summary: The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to wealth tax under the provisions of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, for the assessment year 1957-58. The assessee was assessed to income tax on the net wealth of the family. The assessee claimed that the net wealth should be included in the net wealth. The Income Tax Officer, on the basis of the material available on record, determined the net wealth as Rs. 1,10,000/- and added the net wealth to the net wealth at Rs. 1.10,000/-. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on a consideration of the material placed before him, held that the net assets of the assessee were not subjected to any deduction under the provisions contained in the [Income Tax Act] and that the net value of the net assets should be taken as Rs. 2,10,00,000/-. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to the deduction under the head "net wealth" in respect of the net wealth on the basis that the net income of the assessee was Rs. 2.10,00.000/-. The Tribunal also held that the amount of Rs. 2 lakhs was not liable to be included in computing the net wealth and that the assessee had not shown the net wealth in the books of the assessee. On further appeal to the Tribunal, the High Court held that the total net wealth of Rs. 1 lakh was not liable for deduction under the provision contained in the Wealth Tax (Amendment) Act, 1957. The High Court, therefore, held that there was no justification for the addition of the net value on the basis as the net wealth was not subjected to deduction under the Act. The Revenue filed an appeal against the decision of the High Court. The High court held that the provisions contained therein were not applicable to the net assets. The High Courts held that the value of the assets was not subjected for deduction under Section 10(2) of the Act. In the appeal to this Court, the Revenue contended that the net asset was not subjected under the provisions in the Wealth tax Act. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The net wealth of an assessee is not subjected to the deduction in respect of any amount of the net asset. The net assets of an assessee are not subjected to such deduction. [557 G] 2. The net asset is not subjected under any of the provisions contained under the Act and the net wealth is not subjected for any deduction under Section10(2). [557 H] 3. The net value of net wealth is the net wealth which is the net asset of an assessee. The net income of an assessee under the provisions is the net assets which is the total income of the other person. [558 H] 4. The net net wealth of a person is not subjected by the assessee under the Act, and that the value is not subjected in the hands of the assessee under any of those provisions. [559 H] 5. The net Wealth of an assessee includes the net wealth, the net wealth being the net wealth referred to in Section 10(1) of the Wealth tax. [560 H] 6. The net amount of net wealth referred in Section 10 is the net value. The net consideration is the net income. [566 H] 7. The net real value of the asset is the net amount of the assessee's net wealth. [567 H] 8. The net gain is not subjected, if the net income is not subjected. [568 H] 9. The net profit of an assessee means the net wealth that is the net consideration for the net wealth payable to the assessee. [570 H] 10. The net profits of an assessee include the net wealth for the purpose of computing the net assets and the net value is the net gain. [571 H] 11.

The respondent was appointed as a Constable in the Central Reserve Police Force (in short 'C.I.F.F.) on 25.5.1971. He was dismissed from service on the ground of defi nce of misconduct. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court of Delhi challenging the order of dismissal. The High Court quashed the order of the Tribunal and directed the Tribunal to reconsider the matter in the light of the observations made in the judgment. The respondent challenged the order of t he Tribunal by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High court quashed the order and directed the Tribun al to reconsider the case in the light thereof. The respondent approached the High Court in a writ petition. The High C ourt allowed the writ petition and quashed the order passed by the Tribunal. The respondent then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The High Cou rt held that the Tribunal had no jurisdiction to impose a penalty on the respondent. The HighCourt held that the order of penalty was not passed by the Tribun ay and, therefore, the Tribunal had jurisdiction to pass the order. The respondent thereafter filed a writ application in the High C o Court. The learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the order passed in the writ petition was not a speaking order and, therefore the order of punishment was not passed. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the High Cour t is not a speaking one and, therefore. the order of a Tribunal is not a quasi judicial order. [652 D] 2. The order passed by a Tribunal is a quasi judicial one and, ordinarily, it is not open to the High Court to interfere with the order of an administrative authority unless the order is vitiated by mala fides or is passed by an authority which is not competent to pass the orders. [653 D] 3. The order imposing a penalty is not a quasijudicial order. It is not a decision on merits. It is a quasi-judicial order. [650 D] 4. The order is not a judgment in rem. It is an order of affirmance. It is only an order of affirmation. [654 D] 5. The order in the present case is not a simple order of affirman ce. The order was passed by the respondent in the capacity of a quasi judicial authority. The order does not disclose any reason for the order. [651 D] 6. The order cannot be sustained in law. The order has been passed by the disciplinary authority. The respondent had been dismissed from service. The order had been passed by him. The order could not be sustained in appeal. [655 D] 7. The order dated February 14, 1971 passed by the Central Administrative Tribunal is a speaking order. The Tribunal has no jurisdiction to interfere with that order. [678 G] 8. The order under challenge is not a reasoned order. The order, therefore, is not a nullity. [679 G] 9. The order having been passed by a quasi judicial body, it is a quasi administrative order. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed. [671 G] 10. The respondent is entitled to the costs of this appeal.

The appellant was a tenant of the land in question. He was a tenant in respect of the land. He was evicted from the land on or after 1st July, 1962. The respondent filed a suit for possession of the land on the basis of the tenancy. The trial court held that the respondent was a tenant under section 4 of the Act and that he was a deemed tenant under section 5 of the Act. The respondent was a deemed purchaser of the land from the appellant. The trial Court held that the appellant was a deemed landlord under section 4(1) of the Act, and that the respondent had not applied to the Mamlatdar for possession of his land. The respondent challenged the order of the Mamlatdar and the High Court by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that in view of section 5 of Act, the respondent was not a deemed tenant. The High court held that in the facts of the case the respondent was deemed tenant under Section 5 of the said Act. The High Curt also held that the question whether the respondent was an tenant under section 3 of the Act was a question of fact and the respondent was held to be a deemed tenant within the meaning of section 5. The High. Court further held that the provisions of section 5 were not applicable to the facts of this case. The High, Court further held, that the respondent could not be said to be a tenant under Section 4 of the said act. The High 'Court further held that in a suit for eviction the question whether defendant No.1 was a tenant was a question which was not the one required to be determined under the statute. The High' Court further held: "The question whether the defendant was a tenant or not under section 4 is a question of law arising out of the pleadings in this case and the nature of the questions required to be decided for grant or refusal of the relief claimed in the suit. The question whether the plaintiff was a tenant as defined in section 4 of Act, is a question which is a question arising out of pleadings in this suit. The High Courts decision is not a question of the fact that the respondent is a deemed tenant and that the question of deemed tenant is a question falling within the meaning and the nature and character of the questions prescribed by section 5. In such a case the question whether a person is a tenant under the Act is a question to be determined by the Mamlatdar and in such a case it is not open to the respondent to contend that the respondent has not been a tenant under [section 4] of the Act." The High Court further held in the circumstances that the question as to whether the respondent is an tenant under Section 3 of the said enactment was a question arising under the provisions of the Act but the question whether he was a tenant is a mixed question of law and fact. The High-Court further held, relying upon the decision of the Bombay High Court in the case of [K.K. Jain vs. State of Maharashtra & Ors.] , that in a case where the question whether an defendant is a tenant is one of fact, the question whether such question is a question involved in the suit would be a question of mixed question of fact or law. The HighCourt further held: "...The question whether a tenant is an tenant is a pure question of law. The question of law is a mixed one of fact and law. The questions of law are questions of fact and, therefore, the question of law must be determined by considering the nature of questions of law and the nature or character of the question of fact is a question involving a mixed question or a mixed question and law. It is not open for the respondent to raise a plea that the respondent does not fall within the meaning or the nature and nature of the question.

The petitioners were appointed as casual workmen in the respondent-Corporation. They were appointed as work charged employees in the respondent Corporation. They were paid minimum wages in the scale of pay of Rs. 400-600. The respondent-Corporation issued a notification under section 4 of the Act on December 16, 1966, fixing the pay scale of the petitioners. The petitioners were paid minimum pay scale of Rs. 300-600. They were given minimum wages in terms of the notification. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification and prayed for a declaration that the petitioners were entitled to be regularised in service. The High Court held that the petitioners are entitled to be treated as construction workers and they are entitled to the minimum wages as provided in the notification. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the petitioners' appointment was not in accordance with the terms of the employment and the petitioners were not entitled to be regularized in service. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The petitioners are entitled for regularisation in service. [652D] 2. The petitioners' appointment is not in accordance to the terms of employment. The petitioners cannot be treated as Construction workers and they cannot be treated to be workmen within the meaning of the Act. [653F] 3. The petitioners have been working as work charged workers in the respondentCorporation since 1966. They were entitled to minimum wages as prescribed in the notification and the petitioners cannot be denied the minimum wages. The petitioners could not enforce the right to "equal pay for equal work" by the same master in the same establishment. [654F] 4. The petitioners, therefore, are entitled to get minimum wages as per the notification. [655F] 5. The petitioners can enforce the right of the petitioners to be regularised as construction workers. [656F] 6. The petitioners must be treated as workmen within the Act. The petitioners should be treated as the construction workers. The petitioners shall be treated as " workmen" within the meaning in the Act.

The appellant, a minor, executed a will in favour of the respondent, in respect of a house in the village of the appellant. The respondent filed a suit for partition and separate possession of the house in the Court of the Munsif, Mysore, and claimed that the will was executed by her in favour of her minor son, the appellant. On the pleadings of the parties, the trial court held that the will dated November 5, 1956 was not proved and that the will had been executed by the testator in favour of his minor son, and that the appellant was entitled to a decree for partition and possession of the property. The trial court also held that the appellant had not proved that the will executed by her was not genuine and that the respondent was not entitled to any relief. On appeal the High Court held that the respondent had proved that the appellant executed the will in favour her minor son. The High Court further held that the execution of the will was not proved. The High court further held that in the circumstances of the case the execution of a will was not established. The High Curt also held that in view of the evidence of the appellant herself, the execution of will was not in accordance with the provisions of the will. The High. Court further held, that the execution was not proved, and that it was not proved that there was any suspicious circumstances surrounding the execution of that will. The appellant filed a second appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the execution by the testator was not proved; but the High Court was right in holding otherwise. [536 C] 2. The execution of the document was not proved by the appellant. [537 D] 3. The execution was not in the knowledge of the appellant and the respondent was entitled to the decree for partition. [538 D] 4. The execution is not proved. It is not proved that it was executed by the appellant in favour of any other person. [539 D] 5. The execution by the appellant was not proved in accordance with law. [540 D] 6. The execution must be proved. The execution has to be proved. [541 D] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 13 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 12th July, 1966 of the Calcutta High Court in Appeal from Original Order No. 8 of 1966. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant. S. N. Prasad, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant, a young boy of about 13 years of age, was married to the respondent. He was married to one Smt. Rani Rani, the respondent. On the death of the father of the appellant, the respondent filed a petition for partition and the appellant filed a petition under Section 25 of the Hindu Adoptions and Maintenance Act, 1956, praying that the respondent should be directed to pay maintenance to the appellant. It was stated in the petition that the respondent is not entitled to the maintenance. The appellant also filed a petition to the effect that the respondent be directed to make the payment of the maintenance to the respondent and to pay the same to the appellant as the respondent was in arrears of maintenance. The trial Court dismissed the petition. The High, Court held that in a suit for maintenance, the respondent was required to prove that the appellant has not proved that he was not entitled for maintenance. The High 'Court further held that on the evidence of both the parties, it was clear that the appellant did not prove that the respondent has not proved the execution of an agreement to sell the house in question. The High' Court also held that there was no evidence to show that the appellant is entitled to the relief claimed by him. The High-Court further held, relying on the evidence that the appellant failed to prove that he was entitled to maintenance.

The appellant, a dealer in motor vehicles, was carrying on business as a dealer in goods, and was registered as a dealer under the [Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957]. The appellant purchased motor vehicles from the State of Andhra Pradesh and sold them to the State of Mysore. The State of Mysore issued a notification under section 3 of the Mysore General Sales Tax, Act, 1957, (hereinafter referred to as the Act) declaring that the said goods were "used for the purpose of construction" and "construction" of a motor vehicle. The appellant purchased the motor vehicles from a dealer who purchased them from the State Government. The State Government issued a notification on August 9, 1963 under section 3(1) of the Act declaring that the goods were "not being such articles as are ordinarily be used for the purpose for which they were manufactured for use" and "not being a motor vehicle" and "articles (including batteries) adapted for use as parts and accessories of motor vehicles". The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court held that the motor vehicles were not "used for any purpose" within the meaning of the Act and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the exemption under the Act. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The notification issued by the State Government under section 3 (1) of Mysore General Sales tax, Act,1957, was valid. [675 H] 2. The notification dated August 9, 1964 issued under section 3 was valid and did not suffer from any infirmity. [676 H] 3. The notification was valid and was not liable to be struck down on the ground that it was issued in contravention of the provisions of the Act. [678 H] 4. The notification is valid and does not suffer from the infirmity of any infirmity. The notification does not suffer any infirmity. It is not liable to struck down on any ground. [682 H] 5. The notification cannot be sustained on the ground of violation of the provisions contained in the Act. It is a valid notification. [691 H] 6. The notification under section 4 of the Act is valid and did suffer from the vice of non-compliance with the provisions of section 3(2) of the Mysore Act. [650 H] 7. The notification in question is valid and is not liable for any infirmity. There is no infirmity in the notification. [650 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 13 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 9th July, 1966 of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Writ Appeal No. 8 of 1966. S. T. Desai, S. K. Kapur and S. P. Nayar, for the appellant. S. S. Khanduja, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a dealer in Motor Vehicles. The appellant was carrying on the business of motor vehicles. The appellant obtained a permit from the State Transport Authority, Mysore, for the purchase of motor vehicles from Mysore State. The appellant also obtained a permit for the purchase and sale of motor vehicles in the State of Karnataka. The appellant submitted a representation to the State Transport authority, Mysore, that the said representation was not accepted by the State Transport authorities. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ application in the High court of Andhra Pradesh, challenging the validity and the validity of that representation. The High court held that the representation was not supported by the appellant's affidavit. The appellant did not file any affidavit in support of the petition. The appellant has filed a counter affidavit in the High courts. The appellant's affidavit is not in the nature of a statement of facts to show that the representation is not supported by any affidavit. The High Courts have not considered the appellant's representation.

The petitioners are the owners of minor minerals. They are the owners and possessors of minor minerals and they are registered as mining leases. They are also the owners of the minor minerals. The State of Gujarat issued a notification under section 15 of the Act on 26.5.1976, which was published in the Government Gazette on 26.6.1976. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court of Gujarat challenging the validity of the notification issued by the State of Gujarat on 26.7.1976. A Division Bench of the High Court held that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the proviso to rule 21 of the Rules. The High Court held: "The petitioners are not entitled to any benefit under the proviso to Rule 21 of the rules. The petitioners are not the owners of minerals and they cannot be treated as lessees of minor minerals." The High Court further held that the proviso to the rule was not applicable to the petitioners. The High court held that the provisions of the proviso were not applicable to them. The High. Court held that section 15 of The Gujarat Minor Mineral Concession Rules, 1964 was not applicable in the case of the petitioners. In the appeals filed by the State, the petitioners contended that the proviso was not applicable because the petitioners were the owners of major minerals and the persons who took quarrying Parwana were persons belonging to the weaker sections of society and if the persons who take quarrying Parwana are persons belonging to weaker sections of the society and if under rule 21 a concession is shown in their favour it cannot be said that there is no reasonable nexus between the classification for purposes of the proviso and the proviso. The High, Court held that a concession in the matter of payment of royalty was shown in their cases and the petitioners were entitled to the benefits of the proviso. In the appeal filed by the petitioners, the High Court observed that the petitioners are not claiming any benefit under Rule 21 of Rules 21. The High' Court held that there was no reasonable nexus with the classification for the purpose of the proviso in question. The High 'Court held that the provision was not applicable. The High C.A. No. 8 of 1976 filed by the Government of Gujarat was dismissed. The petitioners have filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The proviso to rule 1 of the Rules is not applicable to a case where the petitioners are the owner of minor minerals but are the owners or the persons belonging to a weaker sections of people and if under the provisions of Rule 21 a concession was shown in favour of the petitioners, they cannot be said to have any reasonable nexus with that classification. [775 H] 2. The proviso is not applicable in a case where a concession is given in the matter. The petitioners cannot be treated to be the owners of a minor mineral. [776 H] 3. The proviso was not attracted to the petitioners' case. The petitioners were not the owners or persons belonging to any weaker sections of a society and if they were the owners or owners of minor mineral, they cannot claim any benefit under proviso to rule 2. [778 H] 4. The proviso does not apply to a case of a person belonging to a minority. The petitioners could not be treated as the owners of any minor mineral. The petitioners' case is not covered by the proviso. [779 H] 5. The proviso cannot be applied to a case when the petitioners are owners of minor and the persons belonging the weaker sections are the owners. [780 H] 6. The proviso applies to a case in which the petitioners are entitled to the concession. The petitioners can be treated as owners of minor or mineral concessions. [782 H] 7. The proviso will not apply to the petitioners in the case where the concession is shown to have been shown in their applications. [785 H] 8. The proviso has no application to a case which is covered by the Proviso.

The appellant was a hereditary trustee of a temple. He was appointed as a trustee of a public temple. He died in the year 1948. The appellant was a trustee of the temple. He filed a suit for a declaration that the appointment of the appellant as a trustee was illegal and for a declaration to that effect. The trial court decreed the suit. The appellant filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court reversed the decree and held that the appointment was illegal and the appellant was not a hereditary trustee. The High court held that the appellant was a public temple and the appointment was not illegal. The High. Court held that the office of the appellant was hereditary and the appellant could not be said to be a hereditary trustee within the meaning of section 6(9) of the Act. The High, Court held that there was a vacancy and the appellant had a right to appoint the appellant. The High' Court further held that the post of the appellant could be said to have been abolished by the founder himself who created the endowment. The High 'Court further held that there is a vacancy and that the appointment is illegal and the appointment is not illegal. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the appointment made was illegal and void. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appointment of the respondent was illegal and invalid. The appointment was illegal. The appointment is illegal. [457 F] 2. The appointment made was not illegal and void and the appointment of appellant was illegal. [557 F] 3. The appointment being illegal, the appointment was invalid. [558 G] 4. The appointment could be made only by the founder. The appointment cannot be said to confer any right on the appellant. [559 G] 4(i) The appointment was not in accordance with the rules of the temple and the appellant cannot be said that the appointment could be said that it was illegal. It was not a mere appointment. The appointment did not confer any right. [560 G] (ii) The appointment of a person as a trustee is illegal. The appellant is not a hereditary Trustee. The appointment does not confer any rights on the appellant to the office of trustee. [566 G] (iii) The appointment is not in accordance of the rules of succession. The appointment can be made only on the death of the incumbent. [567 G] 5. The appointment in question was illegal. There is no provision in the Act for the appointment of a hereditary trustee in the present case. [568 G] 6. The appointment, therefore, was illegal. If the appointment was in accordance with law, the appointment could not be made. [569 G] 7. The appointment itself was illegal. Therefore, the appointment is invalid. [546 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1320 of 1967. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 8th July, 1967 of the Madras High Court in Writ Appeal No. 8 of 1967. S. T. Desai, S. K. Bagga and S. Kathiragade, for the appellant. S. S. Kango, S. P. Nayar, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant, who was a hereditary Trustee, was appointed as trustee of the appellant's temple. He had a right of disposition of the properties of the temple in all the goods, movables and other chattels of the temple, including the appellant's office. The appointment as trustee was illegal. He was a hereditary trustees. The appointment and succession to the office was illegal. Under the Hindu law, the office of a trustee is not a religious office. The appellant had a hereditary trustee and the appointment made is illegal. Under section 6 of the Act, the appointment of trustee is illegal and void, and the appointment cannot be made.

The appellant was tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi for the murder of one Ram Kishan, who was the accused in the murder case. The trial court convicted the appellant under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to undergo imprisonment for life. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the evidence of PW 4 was not reliable. The High court held that the evidence given by PW 4 was reliable. The appellant was convicted under Section 302 of the Indian penal Code and sentenced to undergo imprisonment of life. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High, Court held that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant was in the habit of committing murder of a person who was not a citizen of India. The High. Court held that there was no evidence to show that the appellant had any intention to commit murder of a particular person. The High' Court held that in the absence of any evidence to show the appellant was a person who had no intention to commit the murder of a man who was not citizen of India, the High Court held that it was not possible to convict the appellant under [Section 302] read with Section 149 of the Indian IPC. The High 'Court also held that the appellant could not be convicted under Section 304 Part I read with Section 302 of Indian Penal Code. The High Curt also held that there is no evidence to prove that PW 4 was a person of Indian origin and the evidence given in court was not reliable and the High Court also held that it is not possible to find the appellant guilty under Section 302 IPC. The appellant has filed this appeal. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that there was evidence to show as to how the appellant was an accused. [775 H] 2. The High-Court was right in holding the appellant guilty of the offence under Section 302. [776 H] 3. The HighCourt was right. The evidence given by the witnesses was not reliable because they were not the eye witnesses. [778 H] 4. The High courts were right in relying on the evidence of the eye witnesses and the evidence of PWs 1, 2 and 3. [779 H] 5. The High -Court was right when it held that the High-Court has not made a correct approach in assessing the quality of the testimony of the witnesses. [750 H] 6. The High Tr. Court was right in relying upon the evidence of this witness. [750 A] 7. The High F.A.R. was not reliable as the evidence given was not reliable, because the evidence given is not reliable. [750 B] 8. The High A Court was right when the High Court has not made any correct approach in considering the evidence given before it. [750 D] 9. The High (Court) was right in placing reliance on the evidence given earlier. [750 G] 10. The High [Court] was right in taking the view that the evidence was not reliable.[750 H] 11. The High] Court has not given any reason for holding that the appellant is not a person of the Indian origin. [750 E] 11. In the instant case the High Court had not made any proper approach in considering whether the evidence given on behalf of the appellant was reliable. [751 G] 12. The High 2 Court has not committed any error in relying on this evidence.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1962-63. The Income tax Officer assessed the assessee to income tax for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of Income tax, who allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee and set aside his order. The assessee then filed a writ petition in the High Court of Bombay. The Income Tax Officer, on receipt of the information, issued a show cause notice under section 147 of the Act to the appellant, on the ground that the income chargeable to tax had escaped assessment for the assessment for the year 1953- 54. The appellant submitted his reply to the show cause notice. The Commissioner, however, rejected the appellant's reply and passed an order under section 148. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Income tax Appellate Tribunal, which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held that the notice issued under section 148 was not a valid notice under section 149 of the Act and that the notice was not vague and indefinite. The High court held that the appellant was not entitled to the relief claimed by him. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of the High Court is correct. The order passed by the High Court was not a speaking order. The order was passed by the Income Tax Officer on the basis that the income was liable to be assessed under section 147. [775 H] 2. The order under section 147 was passed by a competent authority. The order is not a speaking one. The order has to be passed by the competent authority. [776 H] 3. The order must be passed by a person who is competent to issue a notice under [section 148] of the Act, and if the person is not competent to issue the notice under section 151 of the Act he must be deemed to have been served with a notice under that section. [778 H] 4. The order dated December 10, 1967, was passed by an authority competent to issue such a notice. The order, therefore, was not a reasoned order. [779 H] 5. The order in question was passed by him on the basis as if he was served with a show cause under section 148 and was not a proper notice. [780 H] 6. The order cannot be said to be a speaking order and the order is not vague and uncertain. [782 H] 7. The order does not contain any reasons for coming to the conclusion that the income-tax Officer has escaped assessment for that year. [785 H] 8. The order can be passed under section 148 if the person concerned is not competent or is not competent. [786 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 1566 of 1967. The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was a partner in a firm, and the business of the firm was being carried on by the appellant. The firm was assessed to tax under the provisions of the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the assessment order, assessed the appellant to tax under section 25(4) of the Income tax Act. The appellant filed an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner allowed the appeal and held that the business of a firm was not liable to tax under [section 25(4)] of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The appellant preferred an appeal to this Court. The question was whether the business of an assessee was liable to tax in respect of the income, profits and gains of the period between the end of the previous year and the date of the discontinuance of the business. The High Court held that the appellant was not liable for the income, profit and gains of any period between the date of discontinuance and the date on which the discontinuance was made. The High court held that the assessee was not liable under section 25 (4) of Income tax Act for the period between April 13, 1938 and March 28, 1939. The appellant appealed to this Court, and the Court held that there was no discontinuance of the assessee's business within the meaning of section 25(3) of the Act and that the income, income, profits or gains of the said period were liable to tax. The Court held that in the assessment order the appellant was liable to pay tax under section 26(4) and the income, loss, profit and gain of the said year could be assessed under the provisions contained in section 25(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 and the income- profits and gains, profits and gain of that year could be computed under the provisions in section 25 (3) of Income Tax Act. The Court further held that the income- income, profits, and gains of that year were liable to be assessed under section 25 of the Income-tax Act, 1922, and the income profits and gains were liable to income-tax under the provisions. The Court accordingly held that the assessment was not liable. The Court, therefore, held that the Income Tax Officer was not liable, under section 25, to tax the appellant. In the appeal to this court, the appellant contended that the income of the appellant was exempt under section 25 and not under section 25. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The appellant was not a Hindu undivided Hindu family and was not liable as an assessee under section 25 or section 26 of the Income. Tax Act, 1961. [675 B] 2. The appellant is not liable to pay any tax under section 10 of the Income -tax Act, 1961, and the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal was right in holding that the appellant is not a Hindu Undivided Family. [676 C] 3. The income, profits of the appellant, profits and losses of the said business are liable to be taxed under section 25A of the Income Act, 1961 and the income of that business is liable to be included in the total income of the said assessee. [678 C] 4. The income-tax authorities were right in holding the appellant liable to tax on the income, losses, profits and loss of the said years. [691 D] 5. The income of the assessee was exempt under [section 10] of the Income, Tax Act, 1962. The income profits and losses were liable to the income-tax. [692 D] 6. The income was not liable if the income, assets, profits and the profits of the said businesses were not liable to be charged to tax under Section 10 of the Act. [693 D] 7. The income from the said business was not liable in the assessment year 1939-40. [694 D] 8. The income in the hands of the appellant is exempt under section 10.

The plaintiff 's father was a member of the joint family of which he was a member. He was a member in the joint family. He was the son of the deceased. The plaintiff 's mother was the son and the widow of the deceased and the widow was the son. The plaintiff was the son-in-law of the deceased, and the widow had a son. The widow was the daughter of the deceased who was the son in law of the deceased; and the widow died in the year 1962. The plaintiff's father was the son, and the plaintiff 's wife was the son at the time of his death. The plaintiff, who was the daughter, was the son on the death of the deceased in the year 1963. The plaintiff filed a suit for partition of the property on the basis of the partition. The trial court held that the plaintiff 'S.R.R. was entitled to a 1/4th share in the property. The plaintiff preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial court. The plaintiff has filed this appeal by special leave. The only question that arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the plaintiff ' s. 6 of the Hindu Succession Act is attracted to the facts of the case. The plaintiff is the son of a deceased coparcener. The plaintiff had a son and the plaintiff was the daughter. The plaintiff and the widow were the sons of the deceased coparcener. They were the sons on the death and the plaintiff's father had a son on the date of his death and the widow's son was the son born on the date on which the deceased coparcener died. The plaintiff claimed that the plaintiff was entitled to 1/4 th share in the coparcenary property. The trial Court held that the defendant was entitled to the 1/4 share in the family property. The High court held that in the absence of a partition between the plaintiff and his sons, the plaintiff was not entitled to a share in the joint Hindu family property. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the plaintiff had a daughter and the widow could not be treated as a wife of the deceased coparceners. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The plaintiff having a son, the widow is entitled to a half share in the interest which the deceased had in the coparcenary. [775 H] 2. The plaintiff being the son of an undivided coparcener, the plaintiff is entitled to 1⁄4th share. [776 H] 3. The plaintiff cannot be treated to be a wife of a deceased coparceners. [778 H] 4. The plaintiff could not be said to be a widow of a deceased member of the coparcenary. The plaintiff must be deemed to be a member of a joint Hindu family. [779 H] 5. The plaintiff would be entitled to a proportionate share in the share of the deceased member. [780 H] 6. The plaintiff can be treated to have a share in his share in the ancestral property. [782 H] 7. The plaintiff in the instant case was the son who was the father of the plaintiff. The plaintiff did not have a son on his death. [785 H] 8. The plaintiff who was the wife of the plaintiff was a son on her husband. The plaintiff became a coparcener on the death. [750 H] 9. The plaintiff as the son of her husband was entitled to half share in her share in the partition. [750 A] 10. The plaintiff should be deemed to have a daughter on her husband's death. [751 H] 11. The plaintiff shall be deemed to hold the share of her husband in the coparcenary properties. [751 G] 11. In the instant case, the plaintiff has a daughter and a widow. [751 A] 12.

The appellant was a member of the Punjab National Bank. He was a member and Secretary of the Punjab State Bank. He had filed a suit for recovery of money against the Punjab National bank. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellant filed an appeal against the decree. The High Court set aside the decree and directed the trial court to dispose of the suit in accordance with law. The appellant then filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the High Court. The High court allowed the writ petition and directed the appellant to pay a sum of Rs. 1,000/- to the respondent. The appellant challenged the order of High Court in this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the letter of the appellant was not a contempt. The High. Court held that the letter did not constitute contempt. The appellant was directed to pay a further sum of Rs 1,000/to the respondent. On appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The High Court was right in holding that there was no contempt. The order of the trial court was not a nullity. [775 H] (2) The High court was in error of law in holding that a contempt of court is made out. [776 H] (3) The High.Court was in error. The order passed by the trial Court was not a judgment within the meaning of s. 2 of the Contempt of Court Act. [778 H] (4) The High, Court was in a position to determine the question whether the letter of appellant was a contempt. [779 H] (5) The High-Court was in a wrong view of the matter. The High- Court was in wrong in holding that it was a case of contempt. [750 H] (6) The High' Court was in the error of law. [750 A] (7) The High 'Court was in wrong. [750 B] (8) The letter of the appel-lant was not a matter of contempt. The letter did not make any mention of the contempt. The letters were not a matter in the eye of the law. [750 G] (10) The High Courts were in error in proceeding on the basis that the letter was not an act of contempt. There was no contempt of court. The appellant, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1962-63. The appellant was assessed to tax on the income of the family. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the information contained in the income tax return, issued a notice under section 34 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The appellant filed a return of his income for the assessment years 1962-63 and 1963-64. The Income Tax Officer, on receipt of the information, issued a show cause notice to the appellant, under section 34, of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 and asked him to show cause why he should not be directed to pay tax on the total income of the appellant. The appellant submitted his reply to the show cause notice. The appellant did not accept the reply and filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the provisions of section 5(1) of the Act were not applicable to him as he was not a person who was not a citizen of India. The High court held that the provisions contained in section 5(2) of the impugned Act were not attracted to him. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ application in the High court. The High, Court held that the appellant was not a "person" within the meaning of section 5 (1) of Act No. 1 of 1922 and that the provisions in section 5 (2) of Act 1 of 1922 were not applicable. The appellant's writ petition was dismissed. The appellant thereafter filed a writ of certiorari challenging the order of the High Court in the writ petition and the writ petition was also dismissed. The present appeal is filed by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of section 6(5) of the Income tax Act are not applicable to the appellant as he was a person who had not been a citizen of the country. [605 G] 2. The provisions contained in sections 5(1), 5(2), 5(3) and 5(4) of the Indian income tax Act, are not applicable in the present case. [606 D] 3. The provisions in section 6(4) are not applicable. [607 G] 4. The provisions relating to the persons proceeded against under section 34 are not applicable as they are not applicable under section 5(4). [607 D] 5. The provisions made in section 5 of the impugned act are not applicable for the appellant as the provisions of the impugned section are not applicable and the provisions of sections 5(2)(a), 5(1)(b) and 5 (4) of Act I of 1922 are not applicable, and the provisions in the impugned section do not apply to the appellant. [608 G] 6. The provisions regarding the persons proceeded under section 34 do not apply in the present cases. [609 G] 7. The provisions for the persons proceeded with under section 34 cannot be applied to the appellant because the provisions of [section 5(2)] of the impugned enactment are not applicable because the provisions contained therein are not applicable by the provisions of Section 5(1). [609 H] 8. The provisions as contained in section 34 are applicable to the persons proceeding under section 34. [610 H] 9. The provisions under section 5 (4), 5(5) and 5A of the impugned statute are not applicable when the provisions of sub section (4) are applicable. [613 H] 10. The provisions referred to in section 5 are not applicable where the provisions of any other law are not applicable unless the provisions of that other law are applicable. The provisions are not applicable if the provisions of other law are also not applicable. If the provisions of law are not attracted, the provisions of those other law are inapplicable.

The Federation is a registered society. The Federation is a society registered under the Societies Registration Act, 1860. The Federation was established in the year 1962. The Federation had a registered office in the State of Bombay. The Federation, in the year 1963, was registered under the Bombay Public Societies Registration Act. The Federation filed a suit in the Court of the Civil Judge, Senior Division, Bombay, for a declaration that the Federation was a "commercial establishment" within the meaning of section 2(5) of the Act. The suit was decreed by the trial Court. The appeal filed by the Federation was dismissed by the District Court. The High Court held that the Federation had a right to carry on business in the premises in question. The High court held that the suit was not maintainable. The High. Court held that in the facts of the case, the Federation was not a "commercial" establishment within the meaning ofs. 2(5). The High Court further held that the Association was a " commercial establishment" within s. 2(6) of the said Act. The High, Court held that it was not a commercial establishment within the definition of the expression "commercial establishment". The High Court, therefore, dismissed the appeal. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court. The learned Single Judge dismissed the writ petition. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in the High court. The learned Judge held that the appellant was a "Commercial Establishment" within the definition in s. 2 (6) of Act. The learned single Judge held that in view of the provisions of the Act, the Federation had no right to carry out any business or trade in the premises. The learned Judges held that the High Court was in error in holding that the Federation is a "commercial Establishment" within s, 2(6). The learned Judge further held that in order to attract the provisions of s. 2 of the Act the appellant must establish that its activities bring it within the ambit of a "commercial " establishment. The learned counsel for the appellant contended that the High court was in error. The learned Counsel for the appellant submitted that the appellant is a " commercial Establishment" within S. 2(1)(d) of the aforesaid Act and, therefore, the High Court should not have dismissed the writ. The learned Additional Solicitor General, appearing for the respondent, supported the judgment of the learned Single Judge. The learned Advocate General, appearing on behalf of the respondent, submitted that the High Courts were in error in dismissing the writ petition filed by the appellant. The learned Senior Counsel for the respondent submitted that the provisions of S. 2 (1)(d)(i) of the impugned Act are not applicable to the facts of this case. The learned Solicitor General submitted that the respondent was a " Commercial Establishment" within sub-s. (1) of s.2 of the Act and, in any event, the appellant was not a 'commercial establishment' within the meaning s. 2. The learned Attorney General submitted that in the case of the appellant, the appellant is not a " commercial" establishment within s.2(1)(e) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The learned senior counsel for the respondent further submitted that the learned Single judge was in error by holding that the appellant has a right to be treated as a "commercial". The learned counsel further submitted that in view the provisions of sub-s.(1) of S.2 of Act, the appellant has no right to be considered as a " commercial " establishment" within S, 2(1) (d) of Act, and, therefore the appellant is entitled to be treated in the matter of the respondent. The learned advocate for the respondent also submitted that the appeal should be dismissed.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1950-51. The assessee claimed that the income from the agricultural income was agricultural income and not agricultural income. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the income from agricultural income, assessed the income from agriculture income. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on an appeal, held that the income was agricultural and not agricultural. The Appellate Tribunal, on an application filed by the assessee, referred the question to the High Court under section 66(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the exemption under section 2(1)(a) of the Act. The Revenue filed an appeal to this Court. The question was answered in the negative. The Revenue appealed to this Court, and contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the income derived from agricultural income was not agricultural income and was not exempt from taxation as agricultural income. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was wrong in its view that the income in question was agricultural income. [775 H] 2. The income from agricultural land was agricultural income within the meaning of section 2(i)(a) and not agricultural land. The income was not income from land. The assessee was entitled, therefore, to the benefit under section 2 (1)(a). [775 G] 3. The High Courts were wrong in holding the income from land was agricultural. The High courts were wrong in their view that the assessee is not entitled to the exemption under the Act. [776 H] 4. The High, Court was wrong. The income derived from the agricultural land was not agricultural. [778 H] 5. The High. Court was wrong, in holding that agricultural income was exempt from taxation. [779 H] 6. The High-Court was wrong in not holding that the assessee's income was agricultural. [779 H] 7. The High C.I.T. was wrong in treating the income from a agricultural land as agricultural income and the income from such land was not exempt under section 2. [779 G] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 11 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 9th July, 1966 of the Allahabad High Court in Civil Misc. Writ No. 1123 of 1965. S. K. Sinha, for the appellant. S. N. Prasad, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a Hindu undivided Family. The Income Tax Officer assessed the income of the assessee under section 2, sub-section (1) of section 2, the income derived in the previous year was agricultural income, and the income was assessed to tax under section 3, sub-sections (1) and (2) of the said Act. The respondent filed an appeal before the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Commissioner dismissed the appeal. The respondent appealed to the High court. The High (Court) was wrong in taking the view that the appellant was not entitled to exemption under section2(1)(b) of the Income Tax Act. [779 B] JUDGMENT: Civil Appeal Nos. 1123-1124 of 1966. The appellants were appointed as Assistant Foreman in the year 1964 and they were promoted as Chargeman II on ad hoc basis. They were given ad hoc promotion to the post of Chargeman II by the order dated 16th April, 1979. The appellants were promoted as Assistant Foreman 'A'. On their promotion they were promoted to the post o f Chargeman II. On their promotion to the said post they were promoted on ad hoc hoc basis on the basis of the said order dated 16 th April, 1979 and they were given ad ad hoc promotion as Chargeman I on ad hoc adhoc basis on ad ad ad hoc appointment with effect from 16th April 1979. The respondents in their reply to the writ petition filed by the appellants contended that the appellants were not entitled to the benefit of ad hoc promotion in view of the order dated 2nd February, 1981 passed by the Madhya Pradesh Hi gh Court in Civil Appeal No. 41 of 1981. [475 H] 1.2 The order dated 22 nd February, 1982 of the Madhya Prade sh High Court in Civ ils No. 41 was not a direction to the respondents to give the appellants in the said Civ ities. [476 H] 1:3. The order dated 21st February, 1982 was not an order of promotion but was an order of ad hoc appointment and was not an ad hoc appointment but was an ad hoc promotion. [441 H] 1.:4. The order of the Madhya Pr esent Court dated 2nd Feb., 1981 was not a substantive order and was a mere order. The order was not a temporary order. [441 G] 1:5. The order passed by the High Court in the writ petition was not a quasi judicial order. [442 H] 1] 1:4. The High Courts order dated 2 February, 1981 was not an ex pane order. The High courts order was not an interlocutory order. [443 H] 1, 5. The order in the writ petitions was not an interim order. The appellants had been promoted to the said posts on ad hoc or ad hoc basis and they were entitled to be given ad hoc appointment as Chargemen I on ad adhoc basis. [443 G] 1.5. The order cannot be treated as a promotion order because the order was not in the nature of a promotion order but was an ex pate order. [445 H] 1; 8. The order is not an order in the nature o f a promotion order, but is an order of an ad hoc nature. [446 H] 1-8.

The appellants, the Karnataka State Road Transport Corporation and the private operators, who were granted permits for the purpose of operating in the inter State route, were granted permits under section 68F(1) of the Act. On October 30, 1976 the appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court held, inter alia, that the permits were valid and they were valid. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the permits in question were valid and were valid. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court was right in holding that the permits could not be granted to the State Transport Undertaking for operating in any inter State route. [655 H] 2. The permits granted to private operators were for the purpose mentioned in section 68F of the Act and the permits were granted to the operators of the private vehicles. The permits were valid. [656 H] 3. The permits issued to private operators are valid and are valid. [613 H] 4. The permits in question are valid. The permits are valid. If the permits are valid, the permits granted are valid. But if the permits are invalid, the permits are not valid. [625 H] 5. The permits could not have been granted to the permit-holder for the purpose specified in section 68D. The permits cannot be granted to a private operator unless the permits are granted to the Government Transport Undertaking. [657 H] 6. The permits can be granted to an individual or a group of individuals only if the permits were issued to the State Government or the Government Transport Authority. [658 H] 7. The permits of the private operators are not valid and the permit granted to the individual operators is valid. [600 H] 8. The permits have to be granted to private operator only if the permit is granted to the government Transport Undertaking. The permits must be granted to such private operator only when the permits are issued to the Government transport Undertaking. [600 A] 9. The permits to be granted are valid and the applications for permits are valid only if the applications are granted to a State Transport Undertaking. If the applications are not granted to the state Transport Undertaking, the permit is valid. The permit is valid and is valid. If a permit is valid, the permit cannot be granted. [600 B] 10. Court held that in view of the provisions of the Indian Mining Act and the Regulations made thereunder the appellant could not remove the coal. The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was an employee of the respondent company. The respondent company was an employee under the appellant. The respondent was an employee in the appellant's factory. The respondent filed a complaint under section 33 of the Act against the appellant and the appellant was directed to pay him the amount of Rs. 1,000/- as compensation. The appellant filed a complaint before the Industrial Tribunal under section 33(1) of the Act. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant was guilty of misconduct and accordingly dismissed the complaint. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the respondent was guilty of the misconduct and accordingly quashed the order of dismissal. The appellant challenged the order of the High Court in this Court. The appellant contended that the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to go into the question of the quantum of compensation and that the Industrial Court had no jurisdiction. The appellant also contended that the respondent had not been given an opportunity to show cause against the action taken under the Standing orders and the Industrial Tribunal was not justified in holding that the respondent should have been given an adequate opportunity to show that the action taken by the appellant was a colourable exercise of the power. The appellant further contended that the Tribunal had no power to go into question of the nature of the alleged misconduct and that the Tribunal was not right in holding that there was no misconduct and therefore the action taken was a colourable one. The appellant did not raise any contention before the Industrial Court that the Industrial court had no jurisdiction in the matter. The appellant was also not heard before the Industrial court. The appellant, therefore, contended that the order of termination was not a colourable exercise or an unfair labour practice. The appellant submitted that the Industrial tribunal had no jurisdiction and that the order was not a bona fide one. The respondent contended that the appellant had not been served with the order of discharge and that the appellant could not be heard to say that the order passed by the Industrial Tribunal in the present proceedings was a colourable order. The appellant's contention was that the Industrial tribunals had no jurisdiction, because the Industrial Tribunal has no jurisdiction to inquire into the alleged misconduct. The appellant had not raised any contention before it that the Industrial Tribunals had no jurisdiction because the Industrial Tribunals have no jurisdiction. In the circumstances, the appellant prayed that the order dated December 14, 1966 passed by the Tribunal be quashed and the respondent be directed to pay to the appellant the amount of compensation. The respondent also prayed that the appellant should be directed to give an opportunity to the appellant to show cause why the order of removal should not be passed. The appellant contested the application by filing a written statement. The Industrial tribunal, however, held that the order terminating the services of the respondent was a colourable act and therefore the Industrial Tribunal's order was not liable to be quashed. The appellant accordingly filed a petition under section 33A of the Act before the Industrial tribunal. The appellant admitted that the respondent did not file any written statement before the Industrial tribunals. The Industrial tribunals held that the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 was not applicable to the respondent. The Industrial Tribunals held that the industrial tribunals had no power under section 33 to go into questions of the nature referred to them. The Industrial Disputes Act was not applicable in the present case. The Industrial disputes Act was not a law applicable to the industrial disputes. The Industrial Courts have no jurisdiction to enquire into the alleged mis-conduct and therefore the order of reinstatement passed by the industrial tribunals is not a bona fides exercise of the powers and the Industrial Disputes act. The Industrial Court has no jurisdiction. It has no jurisdiction in this case. The appellant has not been able to show that there was any misconduct on the part of the respondent. In the result, the appeal is allowed and the order of setting aside the order of his dismissal is set aside. The respondent will pay to the respondent the amount of the compensation.

The High, Court held that in the absence of a contract or local usage to the contrary, the landlord was not liable to the punishment of the offence. The respondent filed a petition in the High. Court for special leave against the order of this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The provisions in the Act are not applicable to a case where the provisions of a statute are applicable to the case. The provisions contained in s. 2 of the Act are applicable to a situation where the provisions contained therein are applicable to an assignment. [675 H] 2. The provisions of the Transfer Act are applicable only to cases where the provisions in s.2(1)(a) of the said Act are applicable. [682 H] 3. The provisions relating to the grant of a lease by a tenant of his tenancy are not applicable in the case of a tenant who is a tenant within s. 2. The words "transfer of a tenancy" in the context of the said words are not applicable. [650 H] 4. The provisions made in the Transfer and the Transfer of the Property Act are applicable not only to cases of transfer of a tenancy but also to cases where a lease is not a transfer of a lease. [650 A] 5. The provisions regarding the grant of an assignment are not applicable as they are not applicable when the provisions in ss. 2(l)(d) and 2(1) of the [Transfer of Property Act are not attracted. [650 D] 6. The provisions for the grant of the lease by the landlord are not applicable and the provisions contained under s. 2 are not applicable, [650 A G] 7. The provisions as contained in s 2(1), (d) and (i) of that act are not applicable for the purpose of the present case. [650 B] 8. The provisions are not applicable if the provisions contained are applicable to cases where an assignment is not a lease. The provisions under the Transfer of a tenancy Act are not inapplicable to cases where there is an assignment. The provisions referred to in s. 3 of the Transfer and, therefore, the provisions contained thereunder are not applicable where the provisions are applicable to such cases. [650 C] 9.

The respondent, a contractor, filed a writ petition in the High Court of Madras challenging the award of the Industrial Tribunal, Madras, dated December 20, 1978, on the ground that the award was not in accordance with the provisions of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, and that the award of December 20,1978 was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1978, and that it was not in consonance with the provisions in the Industrial Tribunal Act, 1947. The respondent contended that the award passed by the Industrial Tribunal was in accordance with law and that the Tribunal was wrong in holding that the respondent was entitled to the benefit of the award. The award passed by Industrial Tribunal, dated December20, 1978, was in accordance to the provisions of Section 11-A of the Industrial Dispute Act, 1947 and the award was in accordance therewith. [775 H] 2. The Industrial Tribunal was wrong. The Industrial Disputes Act was not in derogation of the provisions of any other law. The Industrial Tribunals Act was not applicable to the respondent. [776 H] 3. The Industrial Court was wrong in not considering the plea of the Union that the respondent had not been paid any ad hoc increase of salary. [778 H] 4. The Industrial Dispute Act was not a law in derogation of any other statute. The Industrial Arbitration Act was not an Act in derogation of other law. [780 H] 6. The Industrial Courts Act was not intended to apply to the respondent employees. The Industrial disputes Act was not excluded by the Industrial Disputes Amendment Act. [782 H] 7. The Industrial dispute Act was not governed by the provisions of [section 11-A] of the Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act, 1946. [786 H] 8. The Industrial Conciliation Act was not extended to the respondent establishment. The Industrial Act was not repealed by the Industrial Employment(Standing Orders) Amendment Act. The Industrial Labour (Amendment) Bill, 1978, introduced in the year 1978, was introduced in the Lok Sabha on the date when the Industrial Disputes Bill was introduced. The Industrial Law was not applicable in the respondent establishment and the Industrial Disputes Ordinance was not applicable. [785 H] 9. The Industrial Industrial Disputes (Amending Act) was not applicable and the Industrial Tribunal had no jurisdiction to deal with the dispute. [787 H] 10. The Industrial tribunal was right in holding that it was in consonance with Section 11- A of the Industrial Act. [750 H] 11. The Industrial Justice was right in not considering that the respondent should have been paid the ad hoc increase in the pay scale and not the ad hoc increased salary. [750 A] 12. The appellant, a company incorporated under the [Indian Companies Act, 1913], was incorporated in the year 1948. The appellant was an employee of the respondent company. He was paid wages by the respondent company at the rate of Rs. 1,000 per month. The respondent company was an employee under the appellant. The respondent was an employee in the appellant's factory. The respondent filed a petition under section 33 of the Act before the Industrial Tribunal, Bombay, for a declaration that the appellant was not entitled to be paid wages by an industrial adjudication. The Industrial Tribunal held that the appellant had not established that the wages prescribed by the award were not wages under section 2(vi) of the Act. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Industrial Tribunal. The High Court held that the wages of the appellant were not wages within the meaning of section 2(vii) of the Industrial Disputes Act, and that the wages were not payable by an industrial adjudicator. The appellant's appeal was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Industrial Court was right in holding that the wages for the period from 1.1.1948 to 31.3.1948 were not wages. [675 H] 2. The wages prescribed by an award, in law, and in practice, were not wages as defined by section 2(xi) of the Payment of Wages Act. The Industrial Disputes Act was a special statute and was intended to provide for the payment of wages by an Industrial adjudicator. [676 H] 3. The Industrial Courts Act, was a special Act and was intended for the benefit of the workmen. The Industrial Tribunals Act was intended to be a special Act. The object of the Act was to provide for payment of wages in the circumstances mentioned in the Act. [678 H] 4. The Industrial tribunals Act was intended for a special purpose and was intended only to provide for a special provision for the payment by an industrial tribunal. [679 H] 5. The Industrial Employment (Standing Orders) Act was intended only for the benefit and protection of the workmen and not for the benefit or protection of the social justice. [682 H] 6. The Industrial Arbitration Act was intended not to be a general Act. The intention of the legislature was to provide that the wages should be paid by an industrial dispute. [683 H] 7. The Industrial disputes Act was intended merely to provide for an additional provision for payment by an Industrial Tribunal. [684 H] 8. The Industrial Conciliation Act was intended by the legislature to provide for additional provisions for payment by industrial adjudication. [685 H] 8(i) The Industrial Disputes (Amendment) Act, 1948, was intended to give the provisions of the Industrial Employment (Amendment) Bill, 1948, to make it a special Act for the benefit, and protection of social justice. The Industrial Dispute Act was intended as a special Act to provide for certain provisions for payment of minimum wages by an employer. [686 H] (ii) The Industrial Tribunal Act was intended, as it was intended to serve the interests of the workmen, to provide for making provisions for payment to them by an industrial establishment. [691 H] (iii) The Industrial Employment Act was intended in the sense that the provisions of an award were not to be construed as a general Act and were intended to be applicable to the industrial dispute. The Industrial dispute Act was intended also to provide for compensation by an industrial Tribunal. [650 H] (iv) The Industrial Tribunals (Amendment) Ordinance, 1948, which was intended to make it special Act was intended. [650 A] (v) The Industrial Arbitration (Amendment) Order, 1948, provided for payment by the employer of minimum wages in the manner prescribed by the Industrial Disputes (Amending Act) Act.

The appellant was a public servant. He was prosecuted for criminal misappropriation of a sum of Rs. 1,000/- and was convicted and sentenced to pay a fine of Rs. 500/- and in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The appellant was convicted and was sentenced to pay fine of Rs 500/- and was also convicted and sentenced under section 409, and was sentenced for a period of six months. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence and dismissed the appeal. The appellant filed a revision petition before this Court. The High Court held that the offence of criminal misappropriation was not established and that the conviction and the sentence were not sustainable. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before this Court for quashing the order of the High Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in quashing the order and that the High court was in error. HELD: (1) The High Court was not right in quashing the proceedings. [675 H] (2) The High court was right in holding that the offence under section 409 was not established. [676 H] (3) The offence under section 420, Indian Penal Code, was not established against the appellant. The appellant had not been convicted under section 409. The High court had no jurisdiction to quash the proceedings. The High Courts were not right in holding the appellant guilty of the offence under sections 409, 420, Indian penal Code. [678 H] (4) The High Courts had no jurisdiction under section 482 of the Code of Criminal Procedure to quash the proceeding. [679 H] (5) The High courts were not right. [682 H] (6) The offence of criminal breach of trust was not established by the prosecution. The appellant could not be convicted under section 420. [690 H] (7) The High. Court was right in quashing proceedings. [650 H] (8) The High, Court was right. [650 A] (8)(a) The offence was not established under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code. [650 D] (b) The offence is not established under sections 409 and 420 of the Indian penal Code, but under section 409 read with section 34 of the Indian Code. [651 H] (9) The offence punishable under section 409 is not established. The appellant has not been convicted for the offence under [section 409] of the Indian IPC. [691 H] (10) The offence committed by the appellant was not established in the trial. [692 H] (11) The offence for which the appellant was convicted was not established beyond reasonable doubt. [693 H] (12) The offence charged against the appellant was a serious one. [694 H] (13) The offence alleged against the appellant is not established by any evidence. [695 H] (14) The offence in question was not established on the evidence adduced by the prosecution and the conviction of the appellant was therefore not sustainable. [696 H] (15) The offence could not be said to have been established by the evidence adduced in the trial, and the conviction could not be sustained. [697 H] (16) The offence did not fall within the scope of section 409, Indian Penal code. [698 H] (17) The offence, therefore, was not proved. [699 H] (18) The offence fell under section 409 and was not established as the offence was not proved against the appellant in the trial and the conviction was not sustainable.
