The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in the year 1947. The respondent was a company incorporated in the Indian Companies' Act, 1913. The company was incorporated in 1947. The company had a capital of Rs. 1,50,000/- and the company had a share capital of Rs, 1,50.000/-. The company was formed in 1947. Under the agreement dated March 31, 1947, the company was to pay a sum of Rs. 2,50,00/- to the company. The company paid a sum of money to the company on March 31, 1948. The company also paid a sum to the company in respect of the said sum of money. The company filed a petition under Section 33 of the Act for the determination of the age of retirement at 60. The Tribunal held that the age of superannuation of the workmen was 60. The company, however, filed an appeal before the High Court. The High Court held that the Tribunal was not justified in holding that the age was 60. On a consideration of the evidence on record, the Tribunal held that in the year 1952, the age of the workmen of the company was 60. In the year 1952 the company was incorporated and the company was formed. The company claimed that the age should be fixed at 60. In support of the claim, the company produced a certificate from the Medical Officer of the Hospital, certifying that the age is 60. The High court held that the company was not justified under the circumstances in the circumstances disclosed by the oral and documentary evidence on the record. The High, Court held that in view of the evidence produced by the company, the age was 58. In the circumstances, the High Court held, that the age fixed by the Tribunal was correct. The High. Court further held that the appellant was not justified on the ground that the age at the relevant time was 60. It further held that in any event, the age should have been fixed at 60 and the Tribunal was justified in holding the age of 60. The appellant filed a petition for special leave to appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the age as fixed by the tribunal was not correct. The Tribunal was wrong in holding that in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, the age at which the appellant was entitled to be fixed was not correct and that the Tribunal had erred in holding that it was not justified. The High-Court held that the tribunal was justified in not considering the age of a workman at the relevant date. The High' Court held that there was no evidence to the effect that the age in question was 60. Accordingly, the High. Court held that it was open to the appellant to raise the age of an employee at the relevant period. The appellant, therefore, filed a petition before the High' Court under Section 33(C) of the Act. The High 'Court held that in a case where the age of any workman was 60, the age fixed was not proper. The HighCourt held that there is no evidence to show that the age on the basis of which the age was fixed was not the same as the age on which the appellant is entitled to be assessed at 60. On the question of age, the High'Court held that it is not open to the Tribunal to hold that the age has been fixed at the relevant age. The High Curt held that the question of fixing the age of such a person at the relevant point of time was not open to be decided by the Tribunal. The High,.Court held that even if the age of every workman was 60 the same as that on which the age of his was fixed, the Tribunal was right in holding that he was not justified to fix the age of 58. The High:Court held that as the age of each workman was 60 he was entitled to the benefit of the age fixed for the appellant.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in the year 1948. The appellant was a member of the Indian Companies' Association. The appellant, a member of a registered society, was a member in the year 1964. The appellant filed a petition under section 397 of the Companies Act, 1956, praying for the issue of a direction to the Board of Directors of the appellant to make an investigation into the affairs of the company. The appellant contended that the Board of the appellant was not competent to make an enquiry into the affairs and the affairs of its company and that the Board was not competent under section 237 to make an inquiry into the affairs. The High Court held that the Board had no power to make an order under section 237, and that the High Court was in error in holding that the Board could pass an order under [section 237] to make an inspection of the affairs of a company. The High court held that the appellant was a shareholder in the company and that it was not competent for the Chairman to make an application under section 237 for an investigation into his affairs. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The High Court was right in holding that there was no material before the Board on which it could make an inquiry. [675 H] (ii) The power to make a preliminary inquiry under section 237 is a judicial power and the power to make such an inquiry is not a judicial power. The power to appoint an inquiry officer is a judicial function and the power of the Chairman to decide whether he should make an inquiry is a judicial one. [676 H] (iii) The power of the Board to make an assessment under section 237 cannot be exercised by the Chairman in the exercise of his power under section 237. [678 H] (iv) The power under section 235 to make an appropriate inquiry is a quasi judicial power and it is not a matter of law. [682 H] (v) The power conferred on the Chairman by section 237 is not a quasi judicial function. The power of appointment of an inquiry officer under section 237 can be exercised by him only in the exercise and performance of his power. [683 H] (vi) The power given to the Chairman under section 237 does not include the power to appoint the Chairman to the Board. [685 H] (vii) The power vested in the Chairman under sections 237 to make a report to the Board is a judicial act. [686 H] (viii) The power is not a legislative power. The Board is not a Tribunal. The power under sections 237 is a quasi-judicial power. [613 H] (ix) The power in section 237 is an administrative power. The Chairman is not a statutory authority. [613 G] (x) The power exercised by the Board under section 237 has to be exercised by a Board. [613 F] (xi) The power has to be conferred on the Board. The power is a judicial duty. [613 A] (xii) The power cannot be exercised in the exercise or performance of his powers under section 237 and that the power is not an administrative power and the Chairman is not an appellate authority. [691 H] (xiii) The power can be exercised only in the "judicial power" and not in the "exercise of his power". [613 H;613 A] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 877 of 1966. Appeal by special leave from the judgment and order dated the 29th July, 1966 of the Calcutta High Court in Appeal from Original Order No. 1 of 1964. M. C. Setalvad, S. K. Bose and S. K Mukherjee, for the appellant. S. K Jain, for the respondent. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by Shah, J. The appellant is a company incorporated in the State of West Bengal.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi, for the offence of dacoity and dacoity. The appellants were found guilty of the offence of robbery and were found guilty. The appellants pleaded not guilty to the charge. The learned Additional Sessions Judge held that the appellants were guilty of the offences charged and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for one year. The appellants filed an appeal to the High Court. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The appellants then filed a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution in this Court for a writ of certiorari quashing the order of the Additional Sessions judge. The High court held that the prosecution was not barred by limitation. The High, Court held that the offence was not committed at night by as many as 20 persons and that the appellants had the knowledge of the commission of the offence. The High. Court held that in the facts and circumstances of the case the appellants were not guilty of the charge of dacoity and were, therefore, not guilty of dacoity. The High' Court held that there was no evidence to show that the appellants knew that the offence of theft was committed at night. The High 'Court held that the evidence showed that the appellants did not know that the offence had been committed at night and that they were presumed to be involved in the dacoity. The learned counsel for the appellants contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the appellants could not be convicted for the offence under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code. The High-Court held that there is no evidence to suggest that the appellants ever knew that the offences were committed at night, and that the mere fact that they were found in their houses did not make them the dacoits. The High Curt held that the presumption was drawn in this case and the appellants were, therefore entitled to the benefit of the presumption. The HighCourt further held that the case was not barred under Article 226. The High Courts held that the offences charged were not committed at the time of the commission or the knowledge of such offence. The appellants' appeal was dismissed. The appellants thereafter filed a petition for a writ under Article 226 in the High Court of Delhi. The High (Court held that in view of the fact that the appellants have not been able to establish that they knew that the case had been committed by dacoity, the appellants were entitled to the relief. The High: Court held that it was not open to the appellants to raise the presumption in this case. The High T.A.F. was also wrong in holding the appellants guilty of the charges. The High F.A.R. was also correct in holding that there was nothing to suggest that they knew of the commission. The High S.C.A. was also right in holding that in the circumstances of the cases the presumption was not drawn in this manner. The High Cou rt held that there were no evidence to support the plea of the appellants that the appellants was guilty of dacoity and was not guilty of robbery. The High LC. was wrong in saying that the appellants must have known that the offence under s. 395 of the I.P.C. was committed at a time when the case had not been committed. The High Count was wrong in not holding that the presumption under s. 114 of the Evidence Act was not attracted. The High R Court held that if the appellants knew of the offence, the presumption was certainly not available. The High Appel l Court held that as the appellants knew the offence, they were not guilty. The High Vl l.A.C. held that the conviction was not vitiated on the ground that the appellants failed to establish that the offence charged was committed at the relevant time. The High A Court held that on the basis of the evidence on record the appellants were found in possession of the fruits of the stolen articles. The High O.P. was also found guilty of committing the offence of committing dacoity.

The petitioner was a dealer in poisons in the State of Punjab. He was prosecuted for an offence under section 2 of the Act. The petitioner was prosecuted for the offence under section 3 of the Act and was convicted for the offence of selling poisons. The petitioner filed an appeal against the conviction and sentence. The High Court dismissed the appeal. The petitioner appealed to this Court. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that the petitioner was a manufacturer of poisons and that the petitioner had no power to regulate the import, possession and sale of poisons. [675 H] The High Court has not considered the question whether the petitioner was an absolute right to carry on the same. The High court has not considered whether the petitioner had any power to regulate. The High Courts have not considered whether they have any power to control the import, Possession and sale of the poisons. It is not necessary that the Government should declare the substance as a poison for the purpose of committing murder or mischief by poisoning cattle. The Government has no power to control. The petitioner has no power under the Act to regulate the possession of poisons in any local area in which the use of such poison for the purposes of committing murder is to be regulated. [676 H] The petitioner was a wholesale dealer in poison and was not a dealer for the purpose for which the Act was made. The petitioner had no right to carry out the same. [678 H] The State of Punjab vs The Punjab State, [1963] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 8, referred to. The petitioner is a manufacturer of the poison and he was prosecuted for selling the poisons in contravention of the prescription of medical or veterinary practitioner. The High. Court has not examined the question whether he was an absolute owner of the poison. [682 H] The question whether the Government has no right to regulate the manufacture of poisons was not considered by the High Court. The High-Court has not considered that question. The High Curt has not considered any question of the petitioner having any power to regulation. The High, Court has not dealt with the question whether it has any power to prohibit the import, possess or permit the same. It has not considered as to whether the petitioner has any power under the statute to regulate the importation of poisons for the purpose. [683 H] The notification and the application of the rules to any area would depend on the necessity of the same. If the petitioner had power to regulate his import, possession or sale in that area, the Government has power to regulate it. [684 H] The Government has not considered it necessary that the petitioner should be declared as an absolute owner. The petitioner cannot be considered to have any power under Section 3 of the act. [685 H] The decision in the case of State of Punjab & Ors. vs The Punjab and Haryana, [1963]. Supp. 2S.C. R. 8, relied upon.

The assessee, a firm, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1954-55. The assessee filed a return of his income for the assessment years 1954-55 and 1955-56. The Income tax Officer, on the basis of the material available on record, assessed the assessee to income tax for the assessment period 1954-55, and assessed the assessee as a money lender. The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Tribunal, by its order dated July 29, 1969, set aside the order of the Income tax Officer and directed the Income tax officer to make a fresh assessment in respect of the amount of Rs. 2,68,385/and the amount of interest payable by the Bombay firm. The assessee then applied to the tribunal under section 66(1) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 for a reference of the following question: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the Tribunal was right in law in holding that the debt of Rs.2,68,386/was not a debt within the meaning of section 10(2) (xi) of the Income Tax Act 1922?" The Tribunal answered the question in the negative and in favour of the Department. The assessee preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that the amount in question was not a debt and the Tribunal was wrong in holding that it was a debt within section 10(1) (xi). The High Court, however, held that the Tribunal was not right in holding that there was a debt in the ordinary course of the money lending business of the assessee. The High court held that the assessee was a money lender and was a debtor within the meaning ofs. 10(2)(xi) of that Act and the Tribunal had rightly held that the debt in question was a debt and not a debt. The High, Court, however held that the sum in question was, in fact, a debt within s. 10(1)(xi) and the Tribunal rightly held that it was not a loan made in the ordinary way of the money lender. In the result, the High Court dismissed the appeal. The Revenue has come up in appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have given concurrent findings of fact that the amount was not a money lender within the meaning s. 10 (2) (xii) of the Act. [675 H] 2. The amount in question is not a debt but a loan made by the assessee. [676 H] 3. The amount of loan is not a loan. The amount is not a money lending business. The assessee is a money lender, and is a debtor within s.10(2)(xii) of that act. [678 H] 4. The amount was not borrowed in the ordinary manner of the money-lender. The amount must be a loan. [679 H] 5. The amount borrowed by the assessee is not a real loan. The assessee must be a debtor within S. 10(l)(xi) because the amount is not borrowed in any other manner. [682 H] 6. The amount has to be a loan made for the purpose of the business of the assesee. The amount cannot be a loan or a loan. It is a loan made to the assessee. It is not a creditor within s. 11(2) of the Incometax Act, 1961. [685 H] 7. The amount which is not borrowed is not a capital loan. The question whether the amount is a loan or not is a question of fact. The Tribunal was right. [686 H] 8. The amount, if any, borrowed by the assesee is not a loans made in the normal course of the business. The amount does not form a loan.

The petitioners have filed Special Leave Petitions Nos. 823 and 824 of 1990 against the decision of the Karnataka High Court in Writ Petition No. 823 of 1990. The petitioners have filed the Special Leave Petitions against the decision in the Special Leave Petition Nos. 824 and 824/1990. The petitioners in Special Leave Petition No. 294 of 1990 have filed Special leave petitions Nos. 825 and 826 of 1990. In the Special Leave petitions, the petitioners in Special leave petitions No. 826 and 826/1990 have filed Special Civil Application No. 824 of 1989. The appellant was appointed as a clerk in the Bank on January 1, 1962. He was appointed as an Assistant in the Bank in the scale of pay of Rs. 100/- per month. The appellant was appointed in the scale as an Assistant on January 1,. 1962. On January 2, 1963, he was appointed as Assistant in the scale mentioned in the notification. On January 3, 1963, a notification was issued under s.6 of the Sastry award, which was in force on January 1., 1963. On January 4, 1963, an application was made under s. 7 of the Sastry Awards Act, 1952, for setting aside the award. On January 5, 1963, another notification was issued by the Government under s. 8 of the Sastry Act, which was also in force on the same day. On January 6, 1963, on behalf of the appellant, an application under s.7 of the Sastry awards Act was made. On January 7, 1963, it was stated in the application that the appellant was appointed on January 1 1, 1962 as an Assistant and that he was appointed in that capacity as an Assistant. The appellant, a hotel, was granted a lease of a five Star hotel for a period of five years on a monthly rent of Rs. 1,000/- per annum. The appellant was granted a five Star Hotel lease for a period up to 31.3.1982 for a period not exceeding five years. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the grant of the lease. The High Court held that the lease was not for a period exceeding five years and that the Government was not bound to advertise the land for the purpose. The High court held that the land was not a forest land and that the land did not belong to the Government. The High, Court held that it was not a case of sale of land in the open market and that the sale was not in the public interest. The High. Court held that in the case of a lease by the Government, the Government was bound to advertise and tell the people that it was a very exceptional case where the State had made available to the public that it was being sold in the openmarket. The High 'Court held that the sale of the land was in the public interests and that the State was bound to auction or invite tenders for securing the highest price. The High' Court held that since the land was a forest land, the Government could not advertise the land and invite tenders for the highest price, the Government had to advertise the same and invite tenders. The High Curt also held that the Government had not advertised the land for a particular purpose and that the appellant was not bound by the terms of the lease and the High Court was not in error in holding that the Government could advertise the land. The High-Court held that in view of the fact that the land in the reserved forest was not a Government land, the lease was for a period beyond five years and the Government was entitled to auction or inviting tenders for securing highest price. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court had erred in holding that it was the Government which had advertised the land and that it was in public interest that it was to be auctioned or invited to invite tenders for obtaining the highest price and that the High court was in error in directing the Government to auction or invited tenders for securing a highest price. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were not justified in holding that there was no sale of land by the Government. [775 H] 2. The HighCourt was in error. The Government was bound by the lease and it was not bound under the terms of lease. [776 H] 3. The High courts were not justified on the ground that the sale is not in public interest. [778 H] 4. The High T. Court was in error when it held that the State had not advertised and tell the publical interest was to be decided. [779 H] 5. The High [Court] was in error, because the sale was for a term exceeding five years, and that the lease is not for a term of five years. [780 H] 6. The High L. Court was not justified in directing the State to auction or tender the highest price in the open auction. [782 H] 7. The High F. Court was justified in directing auction or inviting tender for securing the bid of the highest bid. [785 H] 8. The High] Court was in fact justified in directing that the Government should auction or tender for the highest bid and that the Court was not required to go into the question of public interest. It was not a public interest. There was no public interest in the matter. [786 H] 9. The High A Court was not right in directing the government to auction or to tender the highest bid in the open court. [787 H] 10. The High 2. The Government had not published the land for public auction.

The assessee, a Hindu undivided family, was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, for the assessment year 1957-58. The assessee, a partner of the firm, was assessed under the Indian Incometax Act, 1922 for the assessment years 1957-58 and 1958-59. The Income Tax Officer, on the basis of the assessment order, assessed the assessee to income tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, on a reference, held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 10 of the Act. The assessee filed an appeal to the Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the provisions of the Act were not attracted and the sum of Rs. 1,50,000 was not available to the assessee. The Tribunal, however, held that section 10 of that Act did not apply to the gifts of the assessee. On a reference, the High Court held that section 9 of the Act was not attracted and that the assessee had a valid gift of the value of Rs.50,000. The High Court, therefore, allowed the appeal and directed the Tribunal to refer the question in the following terms: "Whether the sum of rupees 1,50.000 was available to the appellant for the assessment of the assessee for the assessment for the assessment period 1957-58, 1958-59 and 1958-60, and if so, the sum of Rupees 1,50000 was available for the assessment." The High Court held, on a consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case, that section 10 did not apply and that the sum of the Rs. 1 lakh was available to be included in the property passing on the death of M. The High court held that section 8 of the Act did not come into play and that the amount of Rs.1,50,00,000 was available in the personal account of the assessee and that the High Court was in error in answering the question in favour of the assessee." The High court, therefore, held that there was no valid gift of Rs. 50,000 to the assessee and the sum was available to him for the assessment. The High, Court, therefore held that section 11 of the Act applied to the gifts made by the assessee. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that section 10 was not attracted to the gifts. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in answering the questions in the manner they did. [557D] 2. The High courts were right in holding that section 10 applied to the gift made by the deceased to his son and to his wife. [558F] 3. The High-Court was right in answering questions in the affirmative. [559F] 4. The High. Court was right in holding, that section 9 applied to the facts of the case. [560F] 4(i) The High Court was right. [566F] 5. The High C.A.T. was right in answer to the question in issue in the affirmative and the question in dispute in the present appeal does not arise. [567F] 5(i) Section 10 of the Income Tax Act is not attracted to a gift made by a deceased to his wife, K, by making a gift of the amount of the value thereof. [568F] 5.(ii) The High Courts had correctly answered the question in question in favour in favour of assessee. [569F] 5 (iii) The High C Court was right, in answering the first question in the affirmative, and the second in the negative. [570F] 5:1. Section 10 of Act is not applicable to the facts in the present case. [546F] 5] 5.1 The High Court has correctly answered the first question.

The appellant was a member of the Bihar Judicial Service. He was appointed as a District Judge in the State of Bihar. He was promoted as a District judge in the year 1962. He was posted as a District and Sessions Judge in the district of Bokaro. He was transferred to the district of Barpeta. On the basis of the recommendation of the High Court, the State Government issued a notification on October 10, 1966, appointing Shri B.K. Patro, the District Judge as the District Judge. The appellant was appointed as District Judge in July, 1966. On the recommendation of Shri B. K. Patro the State Government appointed Shri B.P. Patro as the District and Sessions judge in the district. On the recommendations of the High court, the State government appointed Shri BK. Pattnaik as the District judge in place of Shri BK Patro. On the same day, the State Govt. appointed Shri B K Patro as District Judge. On the expiry of the period of probation, the appellant was confirmed in the post of District Judge. Thereafter, the appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Orissa, which was dismissed by the High Court. On the question of the validity of the order of the High. Court, the High Court held that the order of confirmation of the appellant was not in accordance with the provisions of article 233 of the Constitution and that the High Court was not competent to make the order of appointment. The High Court held, therefore, that the order passed by the High. court was not in conformity with the provisions contained in article 233 of that Constitution. The High court held that the appellant was entitled to be confirmed in the cadre of District Judge and that the order was not in consonance with the provisions in article 233. The High. Court held that under article 233 of this Constitution the High Court has the power to make the appointment, promotion and posting of District Judges. The High, Court held that as the appellant was appointed to the post of a District Judge he was not competent for the post of the law secretary. The High' Court held that in the absence of any provision in the Constitution or in the rules governing the appointment of District Judges, the High court was competent to make an order of appointment, promotion or posting of District Judge in any cadre. The High 'Court held that the High court had the power to appoint the District Judge and the High Court had the power under article 235 to make the appointments, promotion and postings of District Judges and the High court could not make the order as a law secretary. On the other hand, the High.Court held that as there was no provision in the article of the Constitution or the rules governing such appointment, the High 'Court was competent to pass an order of transfer of the District Judge in place of the District and sessions judge. The High-Court held that in view of the provisions contained therein, the order of transfer was not in the prescribed form. The High C.A. No. 8 of 1974 filed by the appellant was dismissed by this Court. The appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court which was also dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ appeal in this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have power to make an appointment, promotion, promotion and transfer of District Judges in the State. [536 C] 2. The High courts have the power to pass an appropriate order of transfer. [537 D] 3. The High [Court] was competent to direct the appointment of the District Judges. [538 D] 4. The High] Court has the right to make an appropriate order. [539 D] 4(i) The High Court has power to make such order as is necessary to make an application to the High Court for the appointment of a District judge.

The appellants, who were the sons of the vendor, and the vendors of the appellants, filed a suit for partition of the properties, which was decreed by the trial court. The appellants filed a suit in the Court of the District Judge, Delhi, for partition of their properties. The trial court held that the appellants were entitled to pre emption under clause 'fourthly' of section 15(1)(b) of the Act. The trial Court held that the sale was of a share out of the joint land or property and was not by all the co sharers. The High Court, however, allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The appellants then filed a second appeal before this Court. The High court held that in view of the provisions of section 15 of the Act, the right of pre emption could not be denied to the appellants. The High, Court held that in the circumstances of the case, the sale was not by the co sharer but by all the other co sharers, and that the sale in favour of the appellants was not by any of the co shares. The High. Court further held that the provisions of Section 15(1) of the Indian Act were not applicable to the case. The High Curt, however, held that the effect of the provisions contained in section 15(l)(b) was that the sale is of a share in the joint land and not of a share. The High 'Court further held that in order to attract the provisions of the Act the sale must be by all the joint land. The High' Court further held, that the sale being of a share of a joint land, the right to pre empt the co sharee could not be defeated by the sons of a co sharer. The High-Court further held, relying on the decision of the Supreme Court in Attam Prakash 's case that the effect and effect of the provision contained in section 5(1)(a) of the Land Acquisition Act was that the right of preemption was not available to the co share. The HighCourt further held: "In the circumstances of this case, the right conferred on the co sharor by the sale is not by all of the co co sharers but by all of them. The effect of the section is that no co sharer is left out. The effect and effect thereof is that no other co shar sharer can claim pre emption in the joint property or the property. The High Courts of Delhi and Delhi have rightly held that the right conferred by section 15(2) of the said Act is not available to any of the other co co sharer and that the right to preemption is not available in the case. In the circumstances of these cases, the High Court was right in holding that the right in the present case was not available. The High Tr. Court further observed that the effect is that no one of the co mpugned sale is by all the members of the vendor or vendors who are specified in the erstwhile first three clauses of section 15 (1)(b). The High Court further held: ". In the circumstances, the sale is held to be of a share only. The High Fr. Court held that it was not open to the sons of one of the vendor to claim pre empt. the right of the co ttner to pre emit the co co co co share and the right to the pre empt is not available. In the result, the appeal is dismissed.

The appellants filed a suit for partition of the property in the Court of the Sub Registrar, who was the original owner of the property. The appellants filed a written statement and contended that the sale deeds were not valid and the sale deeds executed by the alienees were valid and the alienees had no interest in the property. They also contended that the alienees have not received any amount from the alienees and the sale deed was not valid and therefore the suit was not maintainable. The trial Court held that the sale deed executed by the appellants was valid and the alienations were valid and therefore they were not entitled to get the sale deeds cancelled. The appellants preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that as the sale deeds are not valid and they were valid and they are valid and therefore it was not necessary for the appellants to have executed the sale deeds in favour of the alienees. The High court held that the appellants were not entitled for the relief of partition and the sale was valid and therefore there was no question of their being entitled to get any amount from them. The High, Court further held that the alienee had no interest to account for the sale deeds and the sale were valid and there was no need for the alienees to have executed any sale deeds. The High. Court held that in view of the sale deeds the alienees are entitled to get possession of the property and the alienee is entitled to get a decree for partition. The High Curt also held that the alienations were not valid. The High' Court held that since the alienees did not have any interest in the properties, the sale deeds could not be executed. The High 'Court further held that as there was no sale deed in favour of any of the alienee, the sale deed could not be cancelled. The High 2. Court held, that the sale was not valid. In view of the finding that the sale is not valid and that the alienor had no interest, the High Court held, the sale was invalid and the alienor was entitled to get an amount of Rs. 1 lakh from the alienee. The High 1 Court held that there was no valid sale in favour of a alienee and the alienors were not entitled, therefore the sale deeds should be cancelled. In the result, the High Curt held that the sales were valid and accordingly the sale deeds had to be cancelled. On the question of the sale deed, the High court held, that as the alienees failed to comply with the conditions of the sale, the sale could not be set off against the amount of Rs 1 lakh. The High-Court held that the alienation was valid and it was not open to the alienees, therefore the High Court was not justified in cancelling the sale deeds. In the appeal to this Court, the appellants contended that the High Court had erred in holding that the sale in favour the alienees was valid and that there was a valid sale in their favour. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Courts were not justified in interfering with the concurrent findings of fact. [536 C] 2. The High courts were not justified on the ground that the sale transactions were not valid in law. [537 D] 3. The sale deeds were valid and were rightly cancelled. [538 D] 4. The sale deed was valid and was rightly cancelled. The sale was valid. [539 D] 4(i) The sale deeds executed in favour of either of the alienors are valid and the alienation was not valid in the eye of law. [506 D] 5. The sale is valid and the transaction is valid. [506 E] 5. In the instant case, the sale is valid. The sale in favour, the alienees by the alienee are valid and there is no need to cancel the sale deeds on the ground of the sale. [506 G] 6.

The appellant, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was incorporated in the year 1958, and it was registered under the Indian Registration Act, 1908. The company was incorporated under the provisions of the Indian Companies' Act, 1913. The company, which was incorporated under a statute, was incorporated under an Act of the Legislature of the State of Gujarat. The company had a total income of Rs. 1,000 per month. The company claimed that the benefit of the Act should be granted to the workmen for the first two days of sickness under the first proviso to section 49 of the Act. The Tribunal held that the benefit should be granted for the first three days of sickness. The Tribunal, however, held that the workmen should be entitled to the benefit of sick leave for the first one day of sickness. On appeal, the High Court held that the Tribunal was not justified in granting the benefit of 7 days sick leave to the workmen. The appellant, being aggrieved by the decision of the High Court, filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court held, that the benefit could not be granted for a period of two days in the guise of sick leave. The appellant filed a writ appeal against the decision of that Court. The appellant contended that the benefit granted by the Tribunal was a benefit to the workmen and that the Tribunal should not have granted the benefit for a period exceeding two days in a month. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The Tribunal was right in holding that the benefit was not granted for a further period of two weeks. [775 H] 2. The Tribunal had no jurisdiction to grant the benefit for an additional period of two months. The Tribunal could not have granted a benefit for a further time of two weeks in the guise that the benefit would be lost for the first time in the guise. [776 H] 3. The Tribunal should have granted the relief for a period not exceeding two weeks in a month, and that the workmen did not deserve any extra amount of leave for the second period. [778 H] 4. The Tribunal has not committed any error in granting the relief for the first period of two hours sick leave. [779 H] 5. The Tribunal did not commit any error in awarding the benefit for the first five days of sickness in the guise it should have granted a further period for a further periods of two weeks, and that is not a ground for granting the benefit for any period exceeding two weeks. The Tribunal ought to have granted the benefits for a period beyond two weeks. In the circumstances, the Tribunal was right. [780 H] 6. The Tribunal is not justified in awarding the relief for sick leave for a period more than two weeks. As the Tribunal has not done so, the appeal is dismissed. The appellant was detained under section 3(1) of the Conservation of Foreign Exchange and Prevention of Smuggling Activities Act, 1974. The appellant was arrested on the allegation that he was involved in a criminal case under section 3 of the Conservation Act. The appellant filed a petition under section 9 of the Act for the detention of the appellant. The learned Single Judge of the High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Division Bench of the High court. The Division Bench dismissed the appeal. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant contended that the grounds furnished in the petition were vague and not in public interest and that the grounds were vague and did not constitute a ground for the detention. The appellant further contended that the order of detention was not in public interests and that the order was passed in public interest. The appellant also contended that the detaining authority was not justified in passing the order of the detention. Dismissing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The grounds furnished in support of the petition were not vague and not merely vague. The grounds were vague. [775 H] 2. The grounds of detention were vague and the grounds were not vague. The appellant had not made out a case for the detention under section 3. The grounds are vague and not based on any material. [776 H] 3. The order of detention is not in public health. The appellant is not entitled to be furnished the particulars of the grounds on which the detention is based. [778 H] 4. The grounds in the present case were vague and were not in public order. The appellant could not make a proper representation against the detention. [779 H] 5. The grounds contained in the petition did not constitute any ground for the order of his detention. The grounds did not constitute an offence for the purpose of preventing the petitioner from acting in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of the public order. [780 H] 6. The order was not in the public interest. It was passed in the public interests. The appellant's right to make a proper and adequate representation was not affected by the grounds on the ground that the grounds are vague. [750 H] 7. The grounds on which detention is based are not vague. [751 H] 8. The grounds do not constitute a grounds for the detention and the order is not in the Public interest. The grounds cannot be said to be vague. [751 H] 9. The appellant cannot make a proper application for the detention unless the grounds are in the public health. [751 G] 10. The appellant did not make out a case of mala fides. [751 A] 11. The appellant having made out a ground for his detention under section 9, the order of preventive detention was not invalid. [751 B] 12. The appellant, therefore, cannot make a valid application for the release of the appellant under section 9. [751 D] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition No. 8 of 1971. Under Article 32 of the Constitution of India for the enforcement of Fundamental Rights. N. A. Palkhivala and R. N. Sachthey, for the petitioner. S. K. Kapur and R. H. Dhebar, for the respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by RAY, J. This is an application for the enforcement by the appellant of a fundamental right to be furnished with particulars of the facts which are not in the possession of the appellant in the petition. It is not in dispute that the appellant was detained in pursuance of the order of this Court dated December 14, 1970. The appellant made a representation to the Government of India against the order of her detention. The representation was rejected by the Government of the State of Gujarat. The appellant then made a representation against the order. The representation made by the appellant was rejected by a non-speaking order. The order is not a speaking order.

The appellant, a former Ruler of the former Jodhpur State, was a Ruler of the erstwhile State of Jodhpur. He was a Ruler in the former Jodhpur state. He was an Indian citizen. He was assessed to income tax under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, and was assessed to tax on his income. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Rajasthan challenging the validity of the levy of tax on his total income. The High Court held that the levy of the tax on his personal income was not valid and that the appellant was not entitled to claim exemption under the agreement with the Ruler of the latter Jodhpur State. The High court held that the agreement was not a law. The appellant, therefore, filed a writ application in the High court for a writ of mandamus directing the State of Rajasthan to pay tax on his own income. The writ petition was dismissed by the High Court. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The question that arose for consideration was whether the agreement was a law. HELD: (1) The agreement was not an agreement of the Ruler of Jodhpur but was a law and was not a statute. The agreement was a statute. [675 H] (2) The agreement did not create any rights in the property of the Ruler. The agreement did create a right in the property to the Ruler to recover the tax. The agreement created a right in favour of the Ruler to get the tax assessed on his personal property. The agreement could not be enforced in the same way as the agreement was an agreement of a law. [676 H] (3) The agreement in question was not a contract of the Ruler but was a contract of personal property. [678 H] (4) The agreement could be enforced only in the Court of the competent jurisdiction. The agreement in the present case was not a decree. The agreement had been executed by the Ruler of Rajasthan and the appellant was entitled to claim the tax on the income of the property. The appellant was convicted by the trial court for murder of one Ramchander and sentenced to death. The prosecution case was that the appellant was a member of the gang of persons who were members of the gang. The prosecution alleged that the appellant and his companions were members of a gang of persons. The appellant was a gang leader and was a member in the gang. He was a member and was a servant of the gang and was a public servant. The appellant and his companion were members of an gang. The appellant, who was a member, was a member. The appellant's companions were members in the gang and were members of another gang. The gang consisted of persons who had been members of the other gang. The members of the appellant's gang were members of other gang. On the basis of the evidence, the trial court convicted the appellant and sentenced him to death. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in reducing the sentence of death in the case of the appellant. The High Court held that the appellant had committed an offence under Section 302 of the Code and that the appellant could not be convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34 of the Code. The High court held that the prosecution case was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and so the conviction and the sentence were not sustainable. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High, Court held that there was no evidence to show that the appellant or any of his companions had any intention to commit murder. The High. Court held that in the case in hand, the appellant was not a member of a gang and that the evidence showed that he was a member or a member of another gang and that he was also a member of that gang. The High' Court held that it was not necessary to convict the appellant under Section 302, I.P.C. and that the High court was in error. The High- Court held that as the appellant was an active member of the other members of the same gang, the sentence of imprisonment should be reduced to transportation in these two cases. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts were right in holding that the appellant has committed an offence punishable under Section 302. [775 H] 2. The High Curt was in error when it held that the conviction and sentences were not sustainable in the case. [776 H] 3. The High 'Court was in error, because the appellant was the member of the same family. [778 H] 4. The HighCourt was in wrong in interfering with the sentence. [779 H] 4(i) The High Court was right in holding the appellant guilty under Section 302 and sentenced him. [780 H] (ii) The High court was right in interfering with sentence. [750 H] (iii) The High C Court was in wrong. [750 A] (iv) The High Courts should not interfere with the sentence unless there are compelling reasons. [750 B] (v) The High-Court was in a wrong in interfering. [750 D] (vi) The High.Court was in the wrong in interfering in the sentence. The High -Court was in an error in interfering with conviction. The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Central Public Works Department in the year 1962 and were promoted as Assistant Engineers on ad hoc basis. They were promoted as Executive Engineers on ad-hoc basis on ad hoc/temporary basis. They had completed the age of 55 years on the date of their appointment. They were confirmed in the post of Assistant Engineers on the basis of the order of the Government of India dated November 30, 1962. They were appointed as Executive Engineers in the year 1963 and were confirmed in their substantive post on the basis that they were in Class I or Class II service or post. They were, however, not confirmed in the substantive post. They had not completed the age limit of 55 years. They were not confirmed in their officiating post. They, therefore, were not entitled to the pay and allowances as per the provisions of Fundamental Rule 56(j). The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order dated November 30. 1962. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The petitioners filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The petitioners were appointed on ad hoc and temporary basis as Assistant Engineers and they were confirmed in substantive post. The period of probation was not a period of probation. The period was not a break in service. The period during which the petitioners were confirmed was not a continuous period of service. The petitioners had not completed their age of 55. They were entitled to salary and other service allowances payable to them from the date of compulsory retirement till the date of the normal superannuation. [690B] 2. The petitioners could not be reverted to the substantive post without giving them any notice or show cause notice. They were only confirmed in the regular post. They could not be promoted to the substantive posts. [691D] 3. The petitioners' appointment was not a regular appointment. They could be reverted to their substantive post only if they were in the regular service or post and they were not confirmed. [692F] 4. The petitioners cannot be reverted to substantive post without affording them any notice. [693F] 5. The petitioners are not entitled to any salary and allowances as they were not appointed on substantive posts. The petitioners did not hold the post of Executive Engineers in Class I and Class II service. They were also not confirmed in that post. The petitioners, therefore, could not be considered to be confirmed in the officiating post. [694F] 6. The petitioners have not completed their service for the purpose of the proviso to Rule 56(J). The petitioners were not confirmed as Executive Engineers. They were merely confirmed in the posts of Assistant Engineers. The petitioners continued to be confirmed as Executive Engineer in the substantive posts and were confirmed. The petitioners must be deemed to have been confirmed in the service. [695G] 7. The petitioners having been confirmed in substantive posts, they could not be treated to have been appointed in the substantive capacity. The petitioners should be deemed to be confirmed. [650G] 8. The petitioners can be reverted to a substantive post only when they were in service. [650H] 9. The petitioners would be entitled to salary for the period of their probation. [696B] 10. The petitioners shall be deemed to hold the post on substantive post. [650C] 11. The petitioners will be entitled to the salary and allowances payable to the petitioners from the date they were confirmed. [797B] 12. The petitioners may be deemed to continue in service. They shall be deemed not to have been promoted to the post of Superintending Engineer. [650D] JUDGMENT: ORIGINAL JURISDICTION: Writ Petition No. 864 of 1981. Under Article 32 of the Constitution of India. N.A. Bana, for the Petitioners. S.K. Bagga, for the Respondents. The Judgment of the Court was delivered by K.J. N.C.J.

The Life Insurance Corporation of India, the appellant, filed a petition under Section 7 of the Life Insurance Corporation Act, 1956, for the payment of the first premium of the Life insurance policy. The Life Insurance Corporation, the appellant before us, filed a return of the amount paid by the Life Insurance Company to the Life Insurance corporation. The Life insurance policy was issued by the Life insurance Corporation of India on the basis of the proposal made by the deceased. The Life assured died on 11th January, 1961. The Life Assurance Corporation of India filed a petition before the High Court of Calcutta under Section 7 read with Section 7 of The Life Insurance Act, 1956 for the payment to the Life Insured. The High Court held that the Life Insurance Policy was not a contract of insurance between the deceased and the Life Insurance Corpn. and that the Life insurance contract was not a concluded contract. The High court held that the death of the deceased was not a result of any contract of insurance but was a result of a contract of life. The High Curt held that the deceased was entitled to the payment of first premium and that the death was not a case of acceptance of the proposal. The High. Court held that there was a concluded contract of insurance and the Life insurance was not a valid contract of insurance. The High, Court held that in the facts and circumstances of the case there was a contract of policy of insurance between deceased and the Corporation and on that basis the Life Insurance policy was not a binding contract between the deceased. In the circumstances, the High Court held, that the Life Assurance Corporation was not a 'State' within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution and that the High Court was in error in coming to the conclusion that there was an oral contract between the Life Insurance Co. and the deceased. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The Life Assured was a 'State'. The Life Insurance Policy is a contract of personal service between the deceased on the death of a person and the Life Assured. The Life Insured was a person who was a 'consumer' within the definition of the term. [775 H] 2. The Life Life Insurance Corporation is a 'State', and the Life assured is a 'consumer'. The Life Assure Corporation is a person who is a 'Consumer' within the ambit of the Act. [776 H] 3. The Life Policy was not an agreement between the deceased or the Life assured and the Life Insure Corporation of India. The Life Guarantee Corporation of India was a 'state' within the purview of Article 12. [778 H] 4. The Life Declaration of the Life Assure corporation of India was not a document of acceptance of a proposal. The Life Claim Corporation of India had not accepted the proposal. [779 H] 5. The Life Insurer was a 'Consumer'. The Life Assurance Policy was not in the nature of a contract between the life assured and the Corporation. The Life Development Corporation of India is a 'state'. The Life Guarantee corporation of India is not a 'state', and the Corporation is a "State". [778 A] 6. The Life Certificate issued by the Corporation is not a contract between a 'consumer', and the LIC is a 'deficiency' within the scope of the Act and the Life Guarantee Corporation is a State. [780 H] 7. The Life State Insurance Corporation of lndia is a 'Government' within the Act. The Life Corporation of India has not accepted the Life Insurance Policies. The Life Claims Corporation of India cannot be treated as a 'State". [750 H] 8. The Life General Insurance Corporation ofIndia is a 'public authority' within the provisions of the Act, and the Life Assurance Policy is a document of a 'State'." [878 H] 9.

The appellant was a Company, which was a registered company, and was carrying on business as a dealer in oil seeds and oil seeds. The appellant was a registered dealer in oil seed and oil seeds and was assessed to sales tax under the [Indian Income Tax Act, 1922]. The appellant filed a petition for winding up of the Company on the ground that the Company was not entitled to recover the income tax dues from the appellant. The Company filed a petition under section 226 of the Code of Civil Procedure for the issue of a writ of certiorari to quash the order of the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant filed an appeal to this Court. The appellant contended that the High Court was in error in holding that the Company had not become a "final order" within the meaning of article 133(1) (c) since the dispute between the parties was not a "final" order within the meaning Of article 133(2) of the Constitution. Held, that the High court was in error. The order of the Additional Sessions Judge was not a final order within the scope of article 133 (1) (b) of the constitution. The order was not a 'final order' within the meaning ofs. 109 of the Code. The order passed by the High Court in appeal was a final order and the rights in dispute in the suit were not determined. The order in appeal was not a interlocutory order within the ambit of article 133 of the Constitution and the order was not an interlocutory order. The order made by the High court in appeal was an interlocutory order within article 133(3) of the Act. The order under section 109 of the Act was an interlocutory one and the High Court had no jurisdiction to pass an order of the nature contemplated by article 133(4) of the Code, and the order of a High Court in revision was not a decree within the meaning s. 109 of that Code. The High court was not in error in thinking that the order passed by it in appeal was final. The order dated the 8th of April, 1955, was an interlocutory and not an interlocutory one. The order dismissing the appeal was not an order in the nature of an interlocutory order and the order dismissing the application for leave to appeal was not final. The appellant could not have been heard to contend that the order of dismissal of the application for grant of leave to appeal to the High Court could not be said to be an interlocutory order, and the High court could not have passed an order of interim injunction. The order refusing to grant leave to appeal is not an interlocutory and the order is not an interim order. The High Courts order is not interlocutory. The order is an interlocutory order as defined in article 133(5) of the, Constitution. The order rejecting the application for permission to appeal to this court is an interlocutory one, and the appeal is not a continuation of the appeal. The order granting leave to appeal cannot be said to have been an interlocutory order in the sense that the order dismissing an application for leave is an interlocutory and is not an order of interlocutory. The appeal is not maintainable. The order for the grant of leave is an order of an interlocutory nature. The order does not determine the rights of the parties in the suit. The order, therefore, is not an intermediate order. The appeal was not maintainable.

The appellant was appointed as a Head Clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti in 1963. He was appointed as Head Clerk on an ad hoc basis in 1963. The appointment as a Head Clerks was illegal and illegal. The appointment made by the Lohar Panchayat was illegal. It was not a term and condition of service. The appellant, who was the Mahant of the Math, was the Mahant. The appellant was the Mahant in the year 1952. He was a Mahant of the properties of the Math. He was appointed as a Mahant of a Math in the year 1953. He was elected as a Mahant in the said year. He was also a Mahant of an institution. He was given a charge of the properties in the said institution on the basis of a deed of trust executed by the Mahant Shivshankar Yati. The appellant filed a suit for a declaration that the properties in question were the personal property of the Mahant Shivshahankar Yati and for a declaration to that effect. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court held that the properties were the personal properties of the Mahant and the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of the Act. The High court held that the property was the personal property and the appellant had no personal interest in the said properties. The High Curt also held that the appellant was not entitled to the benefits of the Act and that the appellant had not acquired any personal property in the year 1954. The High. Court held that in the year 1959 the appellant was a Mahant and the property was not the personal property. The High, Court held that as the appellant was the head of the Math and the properties were not the personal properties, the appellant was also entitled to the protection under the Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the properties mentioned in the Schedule to the Act were the personal assets of the Mahant. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The properties mentioned in Schedule A to the Act are the personal properties and the appellant is not entitled to any benefit under the Act and the High Court was right in holding that the properties are the personal property belonging to the Mahant Shivsa Shankar Yati. [691 H] 2. The property mentioned in Schedule B to the Act is the personal property, and the appellant has no personal interest therein. The appellant is not a Mahant of any institution. The appellant has no right to the benefit under the provisions of Act. [692 H] 3. The appellant had no right to any benefit in the property. The appellant cannot be said to have acquired any personal interest in personal property in any capacity. [693 H] 4. The property in question is the personal properties. The appellant being a Mahant, he is entitled to the exemption under the Act, and that is the position in regard to those properties. [694 H] 5. The appellant could not be said to be a Mahant of his own institution. The property was the property of the Math Sauna or the deity. The appellant did not acquire any personal interest therein in the said property. The property is the personal income of the Mahant, the appellant is entitled to exemption from the levy. [695 H] 6. The appellant, therefore, is not entitled for the benefit of Section 8 of the Act, because the property in question was the personal properties belonging to the Math Saunakar Yati. In the absence of any personal interest, the appellant cannot be held to have acquired personal interest in his personal property. [696 H] 7. The appellant was the Mahant of the Dera of the D.M.C. The appellant was the Deputy Commissioner of the Doda. He died on November 1, 1962. The appellant filed a suit for possession and management of the Dwara. The suit was decreed by the trial court. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree of the trial court and dismissed the suit. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. The appellant is the Mahant of Dera. He was appointed as a mahant by the appellant in the Dera. The appellant had filed a suit against the Dera for possession and the suit was for possession. The suit filed by the appellant was for possession and in the alternative for management of the dera. The suit of the appellant was dismissed by the trial Court. The appellant then filed a second appeal to the Court of the District Judge, Delhi. The High court allowed the appeal, set aside the judgment of the trial Court and dismissed the appeal. The appellant thereafter filed a second suit for possession. In the suit the appellant claimed that he was the mahant of the Dami and the properties appertaining to it by the appellant were his personal properties. The suit had been decreed by the first appellate court. The High Curt allowed the appeal. Hence this appeal. The only question that arises for consideration in this appeal is whether the appellant was the mahants of Dera and the properties of the D,M.C., and the properties appurtenant to it by virtue of the provisions of the Act. The appellant claimed that the properties appertaining thereto were his personal property. The trial court held that the properties were his personal assets and the appellant was entitled to claim management of the properties. The High. The judgment of the High Court is set aside. The appellant will be entitled to costs.

The petitioners were appointed as Assistant Engineers in the Public Works Department of the Government of Andhra Pradesh. They were promoted as Assistant Engineers on ad hoc basis in the year 1979. They were confirmed in the post of Assistant Engineers on the basis of the recommendations of the Commission. They were given the benefit of the age of retirement from 55 to 58 years. They were, however, not given the benefit under the proviso to Article 309 read with Article 313 of the Constitution. The Government of Andhra, however, issued a notification dated September 17, 1979 amending the Fundamental Rules to the Fundamental Rules. The petitioners challenged the validity of the said notification on the ground that it was violative of Article 14 and Article 16 of the Constitution and was, therefore, not valid in law. The High Court held that the amendment of the Fundamental Rules was not violative of Article 311 (2) of the Constitution as it was not in conformity with the provisions of Article 311 of the Constitution, and that the amendment was not violative either of Article 14 or Article 16 of Constitution. The High court held that the proviso to [Article 309] read with Article 314 of the Constitution was not violative Article 14 or [Article 16] and, therefore, the amendment was valid. The High, Court held that it was not open to the Government to alter the age of superannuation from 55 to58 years. The High. Court held that in the absence of any provision in the Fundamental Rules, the amendment of Fundamental Rules was bad. The High' Court held that there was no violation of Article 14 of the Constitution in the instant case. The High 'Court held that the amendments were not violative of the provisions of the Constitution because they were not in conformity to the provisions of Articles 14 and 16 of the constitution. The High C.A. No. 877 of 1983 filed by the State of Andhra Pradesh was dismissed. The State of Andhra, filed an appeal to this Court. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The proviso to Article 311(2) read with Article 311 of Constitution was not in consonance with the provisions contained in Article 311 of that Constitution. [775 H] 2. The proviso is not violative of any Article of the Constitution but is in conformity with Article 314 read with Article 315 of the Constitution which provides that the Government may alter the conditions to which the conditions of service to which the proviso to that Article applies. [776 H] 3. The proviso does not violate Article 14 or 16 of theConstitution. The proviso cannot be struck down as violative of Article 16. [778 H] 4. The proviso can be struck down only if it is in conformity to Article 314 read along with Article 314. [779 H] 5. The proviso must be read in conformity with Articles 14 and 15 of the Constitution so as to take away the rights conferred by Article 14 or 19 of the Constitution to the extent of the power conferred by Article 311. [780 H] 6. The proviso should be read in consonance with Article 314 and Article 315. [782 H] 7. The proviso, in the instant cases, is not violative either Article 14 or 14 of the constitution and, therefore the proviso is not in conformity. [785 H] 8. The proviso has to be read in accordance with Article 314, and not in conformity therewith. [786 H] JUDGMENT: CIVIL APPELLATE JURISDICTION: Civil Appeal No. 879 of 1983. The appellants, who were the purchasers of raw materials, purchased raw materials from the purchasers and sold them to the purchasers. The purchasers purchased raw materials and sold them in the course of export within the meaning of section 5(3) of the C.S.T. The purchasers sold the raw materials to the purchasers and the purchasers sold the manufactured goods to the purchasers in the course o State. The purchasers filed a return of the sales made by them in the prescribed form. The Sales Tax Officer, who assessed the tax, assessed the tax. The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. The appellants then filed a writ appeal in this Court. The question that arose for consideration was whether the sales made to the purchasers by the purchasers were sales in the course or sale of the goods in the course. of export within section 5(1) of the Central Sales Tax Act, 1956. HELD: The sales made to dealers in the course, of export within Section 5(3)(a) of the Act were not sales in the ordinary course of export. The sales made by the purchasers to the purchasers were not sales within the meaning ofs. 5(3). The sales made in the course were exempt from tax under section 24(1) but were not sales made in course of export outside the territory of India within the meaning s. 5(1). [775 H] The sales made were not sales inside the territory of the State of Rajasthan but were sales in course of inter State trade or commerce. The sales were not sales outside the State of Bihar but were sales outside the territory. The sales in question were not sales of goods within the State of West Bengal but were sales within the State. [775 B] The sales in the case of raw materials were exempt from sales tax under section 5(2) of the said Act. [776 H] The sale in the course was exempt from tax by virtue of section 24(3). [776 B] The sale of raw materials was exempt from sales-tax under section 24. The sales of raw materials made by the assessees were exempt from the tax under section 9(1) and section 24(2). The sales in respect of raw materials which were not exempt from tax were not sales. [778 C] The sales were exempt from taxation under section 24 of the Act. The sales to the purchasers did not attract the tax under the Act. [779 D] The sales of the raw materials were not sales and were not sales under the Act and were not taxable under section 9. [779 E] The sales to dealers were exempt from payment of tax under section 8 of the Act and the sales were not taxable. [779 F] The sales by the purchasers in respect of the raw material were exempt from liability to tax under section 4 of the Act, and the sales made in respect of such raw materials were exempted from tax under the said section. [779 G] The sales effected by the purchasers are exempt from tax. [779 H] The Sales Tax Act was not a law in force in the State of Punjab. The sales effected in the course and the manufacture of goods were exempt from levy of tax under the provisions of the Act or the rules made thereunder. [779 C] The sale by the purchasers of the rawmaterials was exempt from the levy of tax. [780 H] The State of Rajasthan v. The State of Madhya Pradesh, [1961] 1 S.C.R. 869, referred to. The sales by a dealer in the course to the purchasers of goods were not sales by the assessees. The sales are not sales in course or manufacture of goods. The sales, therefore, were not sales to the dealers. [779 A] The sales are exempt from the liability to tax.

The appellant, a registered dealer, was assessed to purchase tax under section 10(b) of the Bombay Sales Tax Act, 1958. The appellant purchased the goods from the respondent, a registered dealers, and the goods were despatched by him to the respondent. The respondent filed a return in respect of the goods on the basis of the returns filed by the appellant. The respondent contended that the goods were purchased by the appellant from the respondent and that the goods had been despatched by him and that the appellant was liable to pay purchase tax under the Bombay Sales tax Act, 1958, and that the respondent was liable to make a false declaration in respect of such goods. The Sales Tax Officer rejected the contention of the respondent and held that the goods purchased by the respondent were not "goods" within the meaning of section 10(a) of the Act. The respondent appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. The Appellate Tribunal held that the respondent had not produced the certificate of the Sales Tax Officer that the goods in question were purchased by him from the respondent. On further appeal, the Tribunal held that in the absence of the certificate of sales tax, the respondent was not liable to pay the purchase tax under article 286(1)(b) of Constitution. The Tribunal held that there was no material before the Sales Tax authorities to show that the goods sold by the appellant were "goods" and that the purchase was not "goods". The Tribunal held, therefore, that the respondent could not be held to have purchased the goods in the circumstances of the case. The appellant filed a special leave petition in this Court. The appellant contended that the certificate of purchase was not a certificate of the sales tax authorities and that the certificate was not a document of sale. The appellant also contended that the respondent purchased the goods and that the purchasing dealer had the intention of the goods being despatched outside the State of Bombay. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The certificate of purchase issued by the Sales Tax Authorities was not a Certificate of the Sales tax authorities. The certificate issued by the sales tax Authorities was not an instrument of sale. [532 G] 2. The certificate was not an agreement of sale. It was not a sale. The certificate in the certificate was an instrument of transfer. [533 G] 3. The certificate under section 8(b) was not a " certificate of sale". The certificate was an agreement of sales. The certificate did not specify the goods purchased. The certificate had to be carried out by the Sales tax authority. The certificate could not be said to be a certificate of sale. Therefore, the certificate was a " certificate" of the Sales-tax authorities. [534 G] 4. The certificate must be a certificate issued by a dealer. The certificate is not a certificate issued under section 8. The certificate has to be carried on by the dealer. [535 G] 5. The certificate cannot be said to have been issued by the dealer to the respondent and the certificate was only a certificate of purchase. The certificate does not specify the sale. The respondent purchased the said goods from the appellant. [536 G] 6. The certificate should be a certificate in the form prescribed by the Sales- tax authorities. [506 G] 7. The certificate given by the Sales. Tax authorities is not a Certificate issued by the authorities. The Certificate is not a "certificate of sale". [536 A] 8. The Certificate of the sales-tax authorities is not an instrument or a certificate of sales-tax. The certificate shows that the goods are "goods" in the circumstances mentioned in section 8(a). [537 G] 9. The certificate being a certificate of a sale, the certificate is not an agreement to sale. [506 B] 10. The certificate can be issued by the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax, Bombay, and the certificate is a certificate of registration. [506 C] 10.

The appellant was married to the respondent on April 1, 1962. The respondent was married to a male child on April 1. 1962. The appellant was married on April 1 and the respondent was born on April 1,. 1962. The marriage between the parties was dissolved by the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955. The respondent filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for maintenance and the trial court passed a decree for maintenance. The appellant filed an appeal against the decree. The High Court allowed the appeal and set aside the decree. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the marriage between the appellant and the respondent had been dissolved by the decree of 1962 and the decree was not a decree for the maintenance of the appellant. HELD: (i) The marriage between both the parties was not dissolved by the marriage between them. The marriage was dissolved by a decree of the court. The decree was not an ex parte decree. The decree of the trial court was not a nullity. The decree passed by the trial court could not be set aside by the High Court. [775 H] (ii) The decree passed in favour of the respondent was a decree for payment of maintenance. The decree for maintenance was not a final decree. The appellant could not claim maintenance under section 127(3) (b) of the Code. The decree could not be executed by the court. [776 H] (iii) The decree was a decree of a court. The appellant had not been divorced by the husband. The decree did not create any right in the appellant to claim maintenance. The respondent had not been evicted from the premises. The decree had not been executed by the husband and the decree had not become final. [778 H] (iv) The decree for payment maintenance was not an order of the court and the decree could not operate to deprive the appellant of the benefit of the decree. [779 H] (v) The decree of eviction was not a mere decree for payment. The decree in favour of respondent was a nullity. [780 H] (vi) The decree could be executed by a court. [750 H] (vii) The decree in the present case was a decree passed by a court and not by a court, and the decree passed by it could not be enforced by the respondent. [750 A] (viii) The decree did create a right in the respondent to claim maintenance under the decree. If the respondent had not claimed under section 127 (3) (a) of the code, the decree could be passed. [750 B] (ix) The decree had become final. The decree having been passed by the court, the decree was a nullity and the decree did not become final by the decree. Therefore, the decree passed in the present proceedings was a nullity, and the respondent could not claim the benefit of section 127(1) of the Act. [750 G] (x) The decree under section 127 was a decree in the nature of a decree for a maintenance. The judgment of the High Court was not a judgment in the eye of the law. [750 D] (xi) The decree dated April 1, 1963 was a decree by a court in the same proceedings. The decree dated May 1, 1963, was a decree on the basis of the decree passed on April 1; 1963. [750 F] (xii) The decree having become final, the respondent could claim maintenance under [section 127(3)] of the Code, and the appellant could not be directed to pay maintenance to the appellant. [750 E] (xiii) The decree, therefore, was a nullity in the eye. [750 C] (xiv) The decree is a nullity. It was not a simple decree.
