The appellant, the respondent, was a tenant of a building in the building in which the building was situated. The respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellant from the building on the ground of arrears of rent. The appellant filed a written statement and contended that the respondent was a tenant in the building and that the appellant was not a tenant in respect of the building. The Rent Controller held that the respondent is a tenant in a building and that he is a tenant under the appellant. The Rent Control Court held that the appellant is a tenant within the meaning of section 64 C. The Rent Appellate Authority held that the relationship of landlord and tenant was not established. The Rent Tribunal held that the landlord was a tenant within section 64 C and that the respondent had not been a tenant in occupation of the building in question. The Rent Authority held that in view of the provisions of section 64C of the Act, the respondent was not a 'tenant' within the meaning ofs. 64 C. It was further held that the Rent Control Court was not competent to go into the question of title to decide the question of tenancy. The appellant preferred an appeal to the High Court. The High Court held that in the absence of a relationship of landlord or a tenant, the question of landlord being a tenant in possession of the building could not be decided in favour of the LIC. The High court held that the question of relationship of landlord/tenant was a mixed question of law and the Rent Control Act was not applicable to the case. The High Curt, however, held that the issue of landlord being not a tenant within s. 64 C was not a mixed question. The High, Court held that as the respondent was admittedly a tenant in an unauthorised occupation of the premises, the question whether the respondent was an 'tenant' in respect of a building could not have been decided in favour or against the appellant. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the High Court was not right in holding that the question whether there was a relationship of a landlord and a tenant was a mixed issue of law and fact. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1. The question of landlord's status as a tenant in relation to the building in dispute was a mixed one. The question whether there is a relationship of the landlord and tenant in relation thereto was a mixed questions of law and facts. [775 H] 2. The question as to whether there is relationship of landlord-tenant in relation to a building in which a building is situated, was a mixed matter of law and on a proper interpretation of the Rent Control Law, the question was a mixed mixed question of fact and law. [776 H] 3. The question that the respondent has to be decided in the light of the provisions contained in the Rent Control Order, is a mixed question and the Rent Controller has no jurisdiction to go into that question. [778 H] 4. The question regarding the relationship of the tenant and the landlord being a mixed question, the question as to the landlord being the tenant in occupation, was a pure question of law. [750 H] 5. The question about the landlord being an 'tenant in occupation of a building, was a question of fact. The question was a pure mixed question of facts and law. The question in the present case was a mixed Question of law and law. It was a mixed fact of law and factual facts. [750 A] 6. The question raised by the respondent was one of fact and not of law. The respondent was a 'tenant in possession of a building. [750 B] 7. The question is whether the respondent is an 'tenant within the meaning s. 64C of Act. [750 D] 8. The question which the respondent has been raised in the present appeal is whether the question of the landlord being not an 'tenant', the question of his being a tenant within S. 64C does not arise. [750 G] 9.

The petitioner was appointed as a Constable in the Central Reserve Police Force (hereinafter referred to as 'the Force') on January 1, 1966. He was promoted as a Head Constable on January 1. 1966. He joined the service on January 1,. 1966. He had completed his probation period on January 1., 1966. He filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of his appointment. The High Court held that the petitioner was not entitled to be promoted as a Constable on January, 1, 1966 and that he was entitled to be considered for promotion as a Head constable on January 1 and that he should be promoted as Head Constable on February 1, 1966, and that the petitioner should be promoted to the post of Head Constable on March 1, 1966 on the basis of the said order. The petitioner filed a writ appeal to this Court. The learned Judges of the High Court held, that the petitioner had not been able to make out a case for interference with the final list. The petitioner was, therefore, not entitled to the benefit of the decision of the Mysore High Court. The petitioner, therefore, filed a writ application in the High court. The learned Judge held that the order of the Mysore State Government was not vitiated on the ground that the petitioner did not make out a ground for interference with his final list. On appeal to this court, HELD: (1) The petitioner was not eligible to be promoted to a post on January 1 in the year 1966. He could not be promoted as an Head Constable on the basis that he was not eligible for promotion. [775 H] (2) The petitioner had not made out a case that he was eligible for promotion as Head Constable. The petitioner had been promoted as Head constable on February 1. 1966, and he was promoted as Head Constables on February 1 and February 2. 1966. The petitioner could not be said to have been promoted as a head constable on February, 1,1966, and that he could not be considered for the promotion as Head constable. [776 H] (3) The petitioner could be considered for being promoted as Head constables on February 1 in the same year. The Madhya Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 was enacted by the Madhya Pradesh Legislature to provide for the development and administration of Special Areas through Special Area Development Authorities. Section 2 of the Act of 1973 provided that the provisions of the Act shall have effect as if the provisions of Chapter III of the Act were in conflict with the provisions of any other law for the time being in force. Section 2(1) of the Act provided that the owner of any land or building or any person who is in occupation of any land shall be liable to pay property tax under the Madhya Pradesh Municipalities (Amendment) Act, 1976. Section 2 (2) provided that the property tax shall be leviable by the State Government on the basis of the value of the land or building and the amount of property tax leviable on the land or buildings. Section 2A provided that the tax shall be levied by the State Legislature on the basis that the owner or occupier of any land has been in occupation of such land. Section 2B provided that the State Legislature had power to make laws for the purpose of imposing property tax on lands and buildings. Section 3 provided that the taxes shall be levied in accordance with the provisions contained in the Madhya Pradesh Municipal Corporation Act, 1956. Section 3(1) provided that "the property tax shall, in relation to the special areas and as from the date of the declaration made by the Parliament in respect of a declared industry, be leviable by that Government". Section 3(2) provided for the levy of property tax on the basis specified in the declaration. Section 3 (3) provided that in the case of a declared industrial undertaking, the owner of the land shall be entitled to the payment of property tax under section 69(d) of the Madhya Pradesh Municipality Act, 1961. Section 3A provided that "no property tax shall have effect in respect of any declared industry" and that the property taxes shall be leviable in accordance with any other law. Section 3B provided that "any property tax shall not be leviable by any other law". Section 3C provided that the amount of the property tax leviable under the Act of 1962 was to be levied by a State Legislature. Section 3C provides that the property Tax shall be leviable on the basis as if the property tax was levied by the Central Government. Section 3D provided that the levy of the property taxes on the basis, of the value or value of the property or the amount of tax leviable on such property was to be assessed by the State legislature. Section 3E provided that the liability of the owner of a declared undertaking to pay property taxes under the Act was to be determined by the State. Section 3F provided that the rate of property tax was to be charged by the State and the rate of the property Tax was to be calculated by the State in the manner provided in the Act. Section 3G provided that the rates of property tax were to be determined in accordance with such principles as may be prescribed. Section 3H provided that the local authority was competent to impose the property tax on any land or buildings or any person in occupation of the land. Section 3J provided that the land or the buildings or any other property tax shall continue to be levied on the basis thereof. Section 3K provided that the Municipal Corporation or the State Government may impose the property taxes in accordance with those principles. Section 3M provided that the Corporation was competent to levy property tax on land and buildings and the amount thereof was to be paid by the State or the Corporation. Section 3N provided that the Municipality was competent to pass a resolution to impose the tax on land or buildings and the Municipal Corporation was competent under the Act to impose the same. Section 3O provided that the imposition of property tax shall in the case referred to in section 3C be in accordance with rules made by the State government. The Mineral Concession Rules of 1949 were framed by the Government of India in exercise of the powers conferred by section 20(1) of the said Act. The Mineral Concession Rules were framed by a notification issued by the Government in the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of India, on July 1, 1945. The said rules provided that the rights created before July 1, 1946, for a period exceeding one year, were valid and enforceable. The Government of India issued a notification in the Ministry's of Home Affairs dated July 1, 1944, under section 20(2) of the Act, declaring that the rights of the Government to terminate the rights created after July 1, 1947, were valid. The said notification was published in the Government Gazette on July 1. 1944. The said notifications were published in the Gazette on July 2, 1944, and the said notifications were issued in exercise of powers conferred by the second proviso to section 20(3) of the Mineral Concession Rules. The said two notifications were published on July 1 and July 1, 1943, respectively. The said Government issued a notification on July 1 1, 1944. The appellant, who was a minor, applied for the grant of a lease of the said lands for a period of one year for a period not exceeding one year. The said application was rejected by the Government. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court of Judicature at Allahabad, which was dismissed. The appellant then filed a writ appeal to this Court. The said appeal was allowed by a learned Single Judge of the High Court, and the order of the Government was set aside. The appellant was directed to pay the amount of compensation to the appellant. The appellant challenged the said order by filing a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution. The learned Single Judge held that the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the second proviso, and that the appellant could not be denied the right to continue in possession of the said land for a period beyond one year. On appeal, the learned Single Judge, who heard the writ petition, held that the said proviso was not applicable to the facts of the case. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the said order. The Division Bench, however, dismissed the appeal, holding that the appellant had not acquired the right to terminate the said rights. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, the Court, HELD: 1. The appellant could not claim the benefit of second proviso to Section 20(3). The appellant could only claim the benefit under the second proviso. [775 H] 2. The proviso to section20(3) is not applicable to a case where the right to the land is created by a landholder on or after the 1st day of July, 1945, for a specified period. The said proviso is not applicable in the facts of this case. [776 H] 3. The appellant had not claimed the benefit of section 20(4) of the Mines and Minerals Concession Rules of 1948. The said rule provides that the rights conferred on the Government to determine the rights created by the said rules are not affected by the second Proviso. [778 H] 4. The appellant cannot claim the benefit thereunder. The appellant is not entitled to the relief claimed by him. [779 H] 5. The appellant can only claim the relief under the second Proviso to Section 20 (3). [778 A] 6. The appellant must be deemed to have acquired the right under the second provision. The appellant having acquired the right, he cannot claim the relief of the second Proviso, and the second proviso cannot be invoked. [780 H] 7. The appellant did not claim the relief in the second proviso and, therefore, the appellant cannot claim any relief under the third proviso.
